In real64: 0 is the time, 2 and 3 the container outputs (position1 of FMU 0, velocity of FMU 1), 1 the local variable of the velocity link, stored at offset 1 (offset 0 is the time).

docs.title: Version History Summary
docs.text: Format Version Tool Version Notable Changes 0 ≤ 1.8.4 Initial format. FMI-2 types only. Simple 1:1 port mapping. 1 ~1.8.x Multi-target fan-out for inputs. Separate MT/profiling lines. 2 1.9 FMI-3 numeric types added. Flags merged. Conversion tables. Sequential mode. 3 1.9.2 Binary and clock types. Clocked I/O sections. Importer clocks (LS-BUS). Event mode. 4 1.9.3 Array variable support via DIM field in all I/O lines. 5 1.9.4 Local variables addressed by their storage offset (<LOCAL_OFFSET>). 6 2.0b1 Model-Exchange support: FMU count split into <nb_fmu_cs> <nb_fmu_me>, ME entries carry <nx> <nz>; ME solver slot. 7 2.0b2 Reset trigger of each embedded FMU after its conversion table. Initialization order of the embedded FMUs.

docs.title: FMI API Call Sequence during container_do_step()
docs.text:
Audience: Developers working on the FMU Container C runtime.

This page documents the sequence of FMI API calls that the container performs on each embedded FMU during a single call to container_do_step().

Prerequisite

This page covers the simulation loop. For the sequence that brings the container up to STEP_MODE (instantiation and initialization), see the Initialization FMI Sequence.

The container alternates between STEP MODE (continuous-time advancement via fmi*DoStep) and EVENT MODE (discrete state updates and clock handling). The diagram below illustrates the sequence for the sequential execution mode; the parallel modes (mono-thread and multi-thread) follow the same logical order but interleave the Set / DoStep / Get phases across all FMUs.

sequenceDiagram
   autonumber
    participant C as Container
    participant F1 as FMU #1
    participant F2 as other FMU #2 (… #N)

    Note over C, F2: [STEP MODE]
    C->>C: datalog_log()
    C->>F1: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(set inputs)
    C->>F2: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(set inputs)

    C->>F1: fmi*DoStep(time, next_step)
    F1-->>C: status + need_event_update

    C->>F2: fmi*DoStep(time, next_step)
    F2-->>C: status + need_event_update

    C->>F1: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(get outputs)
        C->>F2: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(get outputs)
    C->>C: time += next_step

    Note over C, F2: [EVENT MODE]    
    C->>F1: fmi*EnterEventMode()
    C->>F2: fmi*EnterEventMode()

    Note Over C, F2: Activate time based clocks
    C->>F1: fmi3SetClock(vr, true) <br/>for time based clocks 
    C->>F2: fmi3SetClock(vr, true) <br/>for time based clocks

    C->>F1: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(corresponding clocked inputs)
    C->>F2: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(corresponding clocked inputs)

    C->>F1: fmi*GetClock <br/>(output clocks)
    C->>F1: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool <br/>(clocked outputs)

    C->>F2: fmi*GetClock <br/>(output clocks)
    C->>F2: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool <br/>(clocked outputs)

    loop Do While more_event
        Note over C, F2: Gauss-Seidel sweep in configuration order<br/>(Set inputs → UpdateDiscreteStates → Get outputs per FMU)
        C->>F1: fmi*SetClock(vr, true) <br/>(activated clocks)
        C->>F1: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool <br/>(inputs + clocked inputs)
        C->>F1: fmi*UpdateDiscreteStates()
        F1-->>C: nextEventTime, more_event
        C->>F1: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool + fmi*GetClock <br/>(outputs + clocked outputs)

        C->>F2: fmi*SetClock(vr, true) <br/>(activated clocks)
        C->>F2: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool <br/>(inputs + clocked inputs)
        C->>F2: fmi*UpdateDiscreteStates()
        F2-->>C: nextEventTime, more_event
        C->>F2: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool + fmi*GetClock <br/>(outputs + clocked outputs)

        C->>C: datalog_log()
    end

    Note over C, F2: Prepare next scheduled event
    C->>F1: fmi3GetIntervalDecimal()
    C->>F2: fmi3GetIntervalDecimal()
    C->>C: compute next_step

    C->>F1: fmi*EnterStepMode()
    C->>F2: fmi*EnterStepMode()

docs.title: Internal steps and communication step
docs.text:
container_do_step(t, h) makes every internal step [T, T + H] (H = time_step × TS_MULTIPLIER, the multiplier read before each step) that ends before t + h, each one as in the diagram above. When an internal step does not fit (communication step not a multiple of the internal step), it stays pending (container->step_pending):

  • while it is pending, the setters of the container (fmi2Set*, fmi3Set*, except clocks) do not forward the values of the importer: they only update the cache of the port (container_port_t.deferred); the embedded FMU's keep the inputs of T, and their outputs, read by the getters, are those of T;
  • the call of the importer that reaches T + H makes the step, then applies the deferred values (container_apply_deferred()) to the embedded FMU's and to the local variables (TS_MULTIPLIER, reset triggers), for the following steps.

The container is at t + h after every call (reals64[0], its time output).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• fmu_set_inputs / fmu_get_outputs in the C runtime expand into a series of typed FMI calls (fmi2SetReal, fmi3SetFloat64, fmi3SetBoolean, …) according to the ports declared in fmu_io.
  • In the multi-thread parallel mode, fmi*DoStep is executed concurrently on each FMU via per-FMU worker threads, synchronized through mutex_container / mutex_fmu.
  • The EVENT MODE phase is entered only when at least one FMU has reported need_event_update, or when clocks are declared in clocks_list.
  • Inside the more_event loop, FMUs are updated with a Gauss-Seidel sweep in configuration order: each FMU is driven Set inputs → fmi*UpdateDiscreteStates → Get outputs before moving to the next one, so a value produced by FMU i reaches FMU i+1 within the same pass and the outputs read back reflect the freshly updated discrete state.
  • fmi3GetIntervalDecimal() is invoked only for FMUs that own scheduled clocks.

docs.title: FMI API Call Sequence during Container Initialization
docs.text:
Audience: Developers working on the FMU Container C runtime.

This page documents the sequence of FMI API calls that the container performs on each embedded FMU while the container itself is being initialized by the importer (co-simulation master).

The container goes through the standard FMI lifecycle states (INSTANTIATED → INITIALIZATION_MODE → STEP_MODE) and propagates every transition to all embedded FMUs. The diagram below shows the sequence for the sequential execution mode; the parallel modes follow the same logical order.

FMI 2.0 vs FMI 3.0

In FMI 2.0 the importer calls fmi2SetupExperiment() and then fmi2EnterInitializationMode() as two separate calls. In FMI 3.0 there is no SetupExperiment: the tolerance and time information is passed directly to fmi3EnterInitializationMode(). Internally the container routes both flavors through the same container_setup_experiment() / container_enter_initialization_mode() helpers, so the sequence below applies to both versions.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant I as Importer
    participant C as Container
    participant F1 as FMU #1
    participant F2 as other FMU #2 (… #N)

    Note over I, F2: [INSTANTIATED]
    I->>C: fmi*Instantiate()
    C->>C: container_new()
    C->>C: container_configure()<br/>(read container.txt)
    C->>F1: fmi*Instantiate()<br/>(CoSimulation)
    C->>F2: fmi*Instantiate()<br/>(CoSimulation)

    Note over I, F2: Setup experiment (FMI2: fmi2SetupExperiment)
    I->>C: fmi2SetupExperiment(tolerance, startTime, stopTime)
    C->>C: store tolerance / start_time / stop_time
    C->>F1: fmi2SetupExperiment()<br/>(FMI2 only — no-op in FMI3)
    C->>F2: fmi2SetupExperiment()<br/>(FMI2 only — no-op in FMI3)
    Note Over C, F2: Apply "early" start values
    C->>F1: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(start values, early or reset)
    C->>F2: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(start values, early or reset)

    Note over I, F2: [INITIALIZATION MODE]
    I->>C: fmi*EnterInitializationMode()
    C->>F1: fmi*EnterInitializationMode()
    C->>F2: fmi*EnterInitializationMode()
    Note Over C, F2: Apply remaining start values
    C->>F1: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(remaining start values)
    C->>F2: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(remaining start values)
    Note Over I, C: The importer sets the inputs of the container

    I->>C: fmi*ExitInitializationMode()
    Note over C, F2: Propagate the links, FMU after FMU (initialization order of container.txt)
    C->>F1: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(linked inputs)
    C->>F1: fmi*ExitInitializationMode()
    C->>F1: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(outputs; ME: after its event iteration)
    C->>F2: fmi*SetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(linked inputs, from the outputs of F1)
    C->>F2: fmi*ExitInitializationMode()
    C->>F2: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(outputs; ME: after its event iteration)
    Note Over C, F2: FMUs are now in EVENT MODE

    Note Over C, F2: Read initial outputs
    C->>F1: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(outputs + clocked outputs)
    C->>F2: fmi*GetReal/Int/Bool/...<br/>(outputs + clocked outputs)

    Note over C, F2: Resolve discrete states
    loop Do While more_event
        C->>F1: fmi*SetClock(vr, true) + clocked inputs
        C->>F2: fmi*SetClock(vr, true) + clocked inputs
        C->>C: datalog_log()
        C->>F1: fmi*GetClock + clocked outputs
        C->>F2: fmi*GetClock + clocked outputs
        C->>F1: fmi*UpdateDiscreteStates()
        F1-->>C: nextEventTime, more_event
        C->>F2: fmi*UpdateDiscreteStates()
        F2-->>C: nextEventTime, more_event
    end

    Note over C, F2: Prepare first scheduled event
    C->>F1: fmi3GetIntervalDecimal()
    C->>F2: fmi3GetIntervalDecimal()
    C->>C: compute next_step

    Note over I, F2: [STEP MODE]
    C->>F1: fmi*EnterStepMode()
    C->>F2: fmi*EnterStepMode()
    C-->>I: fmi*OK (ready for container_do_step)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• fmi*Instantiate of the embedded FMUs happens inside container_configure(), which is itself called from fmi2Instantiate / fmi3InstantiateCoSimulation. By the time the importer receives the container instance, all embedded FMUs are already instantiated.
  • fmuSetupExperiment() only emits an FMI call for FMI 2.0 FMUs (fmi2SetupExperiment); for FMI 3.0 FMUs it is a no-op since the equivalent parameters are forwarded through fmi3EnterInitializationMode().
  • Start values declared in container.txt are applied in two passes: the early pass (container_set_start_values(early=1)) during setup, and the remaining values (container_set_start_values(early=0)) once the FMUs are in Initialization Mode. Values flagged as reset are (re)applied in both passes.
  • The links between the embedded FMUs are propagated during the initialization, as Simulink does (container_exit_fmus_initialization(), run by fmi*ExitInitializationMode() of the container): in the initialization order written by the builder in container.txt (a topological sort of the FMUs by their links, see container.txt Format), each FMU gets its linked inputs, leaves its Initialization Mode, then its outputs are read for the FMUs after it. An ME FMU is read after its own event iteration (fmi*UpdateDiscreteStates() until no more event), never before its first update of the discrete states.
  • No output is read in Initialization Mode: some FMUs (e.g. generated by Simulink) compute their outputs only when they leave it. Consequences: an output of the container read by its importer before fmi*ExitInitializationMode() is not propagated yet; in a loop of links, the first FMU of the loop in the configuration is initialized with the value the link has before the propagation (the builder logs a warning). Clocks and clocked variables are not propagated. A nested container propagates its own links when its parent makes it leave its Initialization Mode.
  • After fmi*ExitInitializationMode(), the FMUs are in EVENT MODE. The container therefore runs one full container_update_discrete_state() loop (the same loop used during container_do_step()) to settle clocks and discrete states before computing the first next_step.
  • fmi3GetIntervalDecimal() is invoked only for FMUs that own scheduled clocks.
  • Once fmi*EnterStepMode() returns, the container is in STEP_MODE and ready for the first call to container_do_step() (see DoStep FMI Sequence).

docs.title: Native runtime of the container
docs.text: The runtime of a container FMU (container/*.c) is a C library that implements the FMI 2.0 and 3.0 APIs of the container and drives its embedded FMUs. This page describes its conventions.

docs.title: Numeric types
docs.text:
The twelve numeric types of the runtime are listed once, by the X-macro FOR_ALL_NUMERIC_TYPES of fmu.h: X(variable, fmi_type, c_type), e.g. X(uintegers16, UInteger16, uint16_t). A per-type list is an expansion of it, the other types (strings, binaries, clocks) being written explicitly:

#define FREE(variable, fmi_type, c_type) \
    free(container->vr_ ## variable);    \
    free(container-> variable);

    FOR_ALL_NUMERIC_TYPES(FREE)
    FREE(strings, String, char *)
#undef FREE

No separator is inserted between the expansions: each one must be a complete statement or declaration.

docs.title: Logger
docs.text:
Each instance of the container has its own logger, container_t.logger (logger_t: FMI version, callback and environment given by the importer, instance name, debug flag). Several instances in one process do not share anything, and fmi2SetDebugLogging / fmi3SetDebugLogging only change their own instance.

The messages are written with the macros LOGGER_DEBUG(...), LOGGER_WARNING(...) and LOGGER_ERROR(...) of logger.h. They log through the variable logger (const logger_t *) of the calling scope:

fmu_status_t container_do_something(container_t *container) {
    const logger_t *logger = &container->logger;

    LOGGER_ERROR("Container: cannot do something (time=%e).", container->time);
    ...
}

The modules without a container get the logger as a parameter (library_load(), convert_new(), profile_new(), datalog_new()) or through config_file_t.logger; an embedded FMU uses the one of its container (fmu->container->logger). A NULL logger, or a NULL callback (allowed by FMI 3.0), sends no message. The debug messages are sent only when the debug flag is set.

docs.title: Locale
docs.text: The configuration files are read, and the reals of the datalog written, with a decimal dot whatever the locale of the importer, which is never changed: config_c_locale_t (config.h) switches the current thread only (newlocale() / uselocale() on POSIX, _configthreadlocale() on Windows; the datalog uses _fprintf_l() on Windows).

docs.title: Native tests
docs.text:
container/tests holds the C tests of the runtime, built by CMake as container_tests and run by CTest (ctest -C Release --output-on-failure from the build folder, or container_tests <test name> for one test). The sources of the runtime are compiled again with the tests, so that the internal functions can be called.

  • test.h: assertion macros (TEST_ASSERT, TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_INT); a test is a function that returns 0 on success, registered in the table of test_main.c.
  • stub_fmu.c: an FMI 2.0 Co-Simulation FMU built with the tests. Its behaviour depends on the GUID given to fmi2Instantiate (e.g. {stub-fail-instantiate}); each type has 16 variables, any other VR is an error.
  • Fixtures: tests/data/one_fmu/container.txt.in is turned by CMake (container_fixture()) into <build folder>/fixtures/<name>/container.txt, with the stub FMU in 00/binaries/<platform>/. The tests of malformed files (test_malformed.c) rewrite one line of the fixture one_fmu into the fixture malformed.

docs.title: Sanitizers
docs.text: With -DFMUTOOL_SANITIZE=ON (GCC, Clang), the runtime and its tests are built with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer; any undefined behaviour aborts. The CI job sanitizers (Linux) runs the C tests with the leak detection, then the integration tests with the instrumented linux64 runtime, the ASan runtime being loaded first in Python (LD_PRELOAD).

docs.title: Common Use Cases
docs.text: This guide presents practical solutions to frequently encountered problems when manipulating FMUs.

docs.title: Change Naming Convention
docs.text:
Problem: Convert from CamelCase to snake_case for all ports.

CLI Solution 
# 1. Export list
fmutool -input OldModel.fmu -dump-csv old_names.csv

# 2. Use Python to convert
python convert_names.py old_names.csv new_names.csv

# 3. Apply
fmutool -input OldModel.fmu -rename-from-csv new_names.csv -output new_model.fmu

Python Script convert_names.py:

import pandas as pd
import re

def camel_to_snake(name):
    """Convert CamelCase to snake_case."""
    s1 = re.sub('(.)([A-Z][a-z]+)', r'\1_\2', name)
    return re.sub('([a-z0-9])([A-Z])', r'\1_\2', s1).lower()

# Read CSV
df = pd.read_csv('old_names.csv', sep=';')

# Convert names
df['newName'] = df['name'].apply(camel_to_snake)

# Save
df.to_csv('new_names.csv', sep=';', index=False)
print("✓ Conversion complete")

docs.title: Remove Debug Variables
docs.text:
Problem: Remove all debug variables before distribution.

CLI SolutionPython API Solution 
# Remove everything containing "debug" or "test"
fmutool -input model_dev.fmu \
  -remove-regexp ".*[Dd]ebug.*" \
  -remove-regexp ".*[Tt]est.*" \
  -output model_release.fmu

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU, OperationRemoveRegexp

fmu = FMU("model_dev.fmu")

fmu.apply_operation(OperationRemoveRegexp(r".*[Dd]ebug.*"))
fmu.apply_operation(OperationRemoveRegexp(r".*[Tt]est.*"))

fmu.repack("model_release.fmu")

docs.title: Simplify Deep Hierarchy
docs.text:
Problem: Reduce Level1.Level2.Level3.Variable hierarchy to Level3.Variable.

CLI SolutionPython API Solution 
fmutool -input deep.fmu \
  -remove-toplevel \
  -remove-toplevel \
  -output flat.fmu

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU, OperationMergeTopLevel

fmu = FMU("deep.fmu")

fmu.apply_operation(OperationMergeTopLevel()) # remove first level
fmu.apply_operation(OperationMergeTopLevel()) # remove second level

fmu.repack("flat.fmu")

docs.title: Extract Only Tunable Parameters
docs.text:
Problem: Create FMU containing only adjustable parameters.

CLI SolutionPython API Solution 
fmutool -input complete_model.fmu \
  -only-parameters \
  -dump-csv parameters.csv

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU, OperationSaveNamesToCSV

fmu = FMU("complete_model.fmu")
fmu.apply_operation(OperationSaveNamesToCSV("parameter.csv"), apply_on=["parameter"])

docs.title: Add Multi-Platform Support (Windows)
docs.text:
Problem: 32-bit FMU must also work in 64-bit.

CLI SolutionPython API Solution 
fmutool -input model_win32.fmu \
  -add-remoting-win64 \
  -output model_dual.fmu

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU
from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.remoting import OperationAddRemotingWin64

fmu = FMU("model_win32.fmu")
fmu.apply_operation(OperationAddRemotingWin64())
fmu.repack("model_dual.fmu")

docs.title: Prepare FMU for Distribution
docs.text:
Problem: Completely clean FMU before public distribution.

CLI SolutionPython API Solution 
fmutool -input internal_model.fmu \
  -remove-all \
  -only-locals \
  -remove-sources \
  -output public_model.fmu

# Verify
fmutool -input public_model.fmu -check

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU, OperationRemoveSources, OperationRemoveRegexp
from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.checker import OperationGenericCheck

fmu = FMU("internal_model.fmu")
fmu.apply_operation(OperationRemoveSources())
fmu.apply_operation(OperationRemoveRegexp(r".*"), apply_on=["local"])
fmu.apply_operation(OperationGenericCheck())
fmu.repack("public_model.fmu")

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
1. Always keep original - Never overwrite source FMU
  2. Test progressively - Apply and verify one modification at a time
  3. Validate after each step - Use -check or OperationGenericCheck()
  4. Document transformations - Create reusable scripts
  5. Version FMUs - Use version control system

docs.title: Pre-Distribution Checklist
docs.text:
• Remove internal variables (^_.*)
  • Remove debug variables
  • Remove sources if necessary
  • Check FMI compliance (-check)
  • Test in target environment
  • Generate documentation
  • Version the FMU

For more examples and support: - 📚 Complete Documentation - 🐛 GitHub Issues

docs.title: From Simulink to an FMU Container
docs.text:
This page explains how to turn an assembly of FMUs built in Simulink (FMU blocks of Simulink Extras / FMU Import, Co-Simulation) into an equivalent FMU Container, and what to check so that both give the same results.

The behaviours described here were measured on MATLAB R2024b with FMI 2.0 Co-Simulation FMUs, by tracing the FMI calls received by the FMUs in both importers.

docs.title: Mapping of the concepts
docs.text:
Simulink FMU Container (JSON description) FMU block an entry of fmu Several FMU blocks on the same FMU file instances: one name per block in fmu, its file in path Line between two FMU blocks link: [from_fmu, output, to_fmu, input] Root Inport feeding FMU inputs input: [name, fmu, input] (one entry per FMU input it feeds) Root Outport output: [fmu, output, name] Output connected to a Terminator, or left unconnected drop: [fmu, output], or auto_output: false Subsystem nested container (container list) Value of an FMU parameter in the block dialog start: [fmu, parameter, value] Start value of an FMU input start: [fmu, input, value] Sample time of the FMU block (FMUSampleTime) and fixed step of the solver step_size of the container (see Sample times) FMU blocks of different sample times one sub-container per sample time, with its own step_size (see One sub-container per sample time) Single-tasking / multi-tasking no equivalent; mt runs the FMUs in parallel threads (see Computation time)

Declare everything explicitly: set auto_link, auto_input (and possibly auto_output) to false, so that the container does not add links or ports that the Simulink model does not have.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A Simulink model with three FMU blocks:

  • fast (fast.fmu, sample time 0.01 s), medium (medium.fmu, 0.02 s), slow (slow.fmu, 0.05 s);
  • lines fast/y → medium/u, medium/y → slow/u, slow/y → fast/u;
  • a root Inport command feeding fast/command, a root Outport result on slow/result;
  • in the dialog of medium, the parameter gain set to 2;
  • fixed-step solver, step 0.01 s.

Equivalent container description assembly.json:

{
  "name": "assembly.fmu",
  "step_size": 0.01,
  "auto_link": false,
  "auto_input": false,
  "auto_output": false,
  "fmu": ["fast.fmu", "medium.fmu", "slow.fmu"],
  "link": [
    ["fast.fmu", "y", "medium.fmu", "u"],
    ["medium.fmu", "y", "slow.fmu", "u"],
    ["slow.fmu", "y", "fast.fmu", "u"]
  ],
  "input": [["command", "fast.fmu", "command"]],
  "output": [["slow.fmu", "result", "result"]],
  "start": [["medium.fmu", "gain", 2]]
}

fmucontainer -container assembly.json

The choice of step_size (here the fastest sample time) is discussed in Sample times.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
Both propagate the links during the initialization: an FMU whose initial state, or calculated parameters, depend on its inputs is initialized with the values of the FMUs upstream (see Initialization of the embedded FMU's). On a chain of three FMUs whose initial outputs depend on their inputs, the container and Simulink give the same initial values and the same values at every step, once the unconnected inputs have the value Simulink imposes (see below).

Both follow the same rule: in the order of the connections, each FMU gets its inputs from the FMUs before it, leaves its Initialization Mode, then its outputs are read. Simulink sets the parameters of every FMU block first, and enters the Initialization Mode of each block just before initializing it; the container enters the Initialization Mode of all its FMUs at once. Neither solves a loop of links at the initialization: the container cuts it before its first FMU in the description (warning at the build).

The unconnected inputs also take part in the initialization: give them the value of Simulink (0) to get the same initial values. An input left at another start value in the container shifts the initial values of every FMU downstream.

docs.title: Unconnected inputs
docs.text:
Simulink sets an unconnected input of an FMU block to 0, in Initialization Mode and before every step: the start value declared by the FMU is not used. The container keeps the start value of the FMU (or the start value of the description) for an input that is neither connected nor exposed.

To reproduce the Simulink model, give each unconnected input an explicit start value of 0 in the start block.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Simulink sets every parameter of the FMU (with its default value when the dialog does not change it) before fmi2SetupExperiment; the container only sets the values of the start block, after fmi2SetupExperiment. For an FMU that relies on its declared start values, both are equivalent. Simulink also calls fmi2SetupExperiment with a tolerance of 0.001 (the container: 1e-8), which matters only for FMUs that use the tolerance internally.

docs.title: Sample times
docs.text:
Simulink steps each FMU block at its own sample time, and holds its outputs between two steps when they feed a block of another rate. The container has a single time step: every embedded FMU is stepped with the step of the container.

  • Without step_size, the container uses the least common multiple of the step sizes of the FMUs that require a fixed step (see Default time step): in the example, 0.1 s; every FMU then exchanges its values every 0.1 s, and fast receives steps of 0.1 s instead of 0.01 s.
  • With step_size equal to the fastest sample time (0.01 s in the example), the exchanges happen as often as in Simulink, but medium and slow receive steps of 0.01 s instead of 0.02 s and 0.05 s.

An FMU that cannot handle another step size than its own (canHandleVariableCommunicationStepSize="false" and a strict implementation) cannot be stepped correctly by such a container: the container reports a warning for each FMU whose step size does not divide its step. Use one sub-container per sample time.

docs.title: One sub-container per sample time
docs.text:
Each nested container has its own step_size and steps its FMUs with it: group the FMUs of each Simulink sample time in a sub-container, and connect the sub-containers in the parent container. For the worked example:

{
  "name": "assembly.fmu",
  "step_size": 0.01,
  "auto_link": false,
  "auto_input": false,
  "auto_output": false,
  "container": [
    {"name": "fast_rate.fmu", "step_size": 0.01, "auto_link": false, "auto_input": false, "auto_output": false,
     "fmu": ["fast.fmu"],
     "input": [["command", "fast.fmu", "command"], ["u", "fast.fmu", "u"]],
     "output": [["fast.fmu", "y", "y"]]},
    {"name": "medium_rate.fmu", "step_size": 0.02, "auto_link": false, "auto_input": false, "auto_output": false,
     "fmu": ["medium.fmu"],
     "input": [["u", "medium.fmu", "u"]],
     "output": [["medium.fmu", "y", "y"]],
     "start": [["medium.fmu", "gain", 2]]},
    {"name": "slow_rate.fmu", "step_size": 0.05, "auto_link": false, "auto_input": false, "auto_output": false,
     "fmu": ["slow.fmu"],
     "input": [["u", "slow.fmu", "u"]],
     "output": [["slow.fmu", "y", "y"], ["slow.fmu", "result", "result"]]}
  ],
  "link": [
    ["fast_rate.fmu", "y", "medium_rate.fmu", "u"],
    ["medium_rate.fmu", "y", "slow_rate.fmu", "u"],
    ["slow_rate.fmu", "y", "fast_rate.fmu", "u"]
  ],
  "input": [["command", "fast_rate.fmu", "command"]],
  "output": [["slow_rate.fmu", "result", "result"]]
}
  • Every FMU receives its own step size, as in Simulink: fast 0.01 s, medium 0.02 s, slow 0.05 s.
  • Give the parent container the fastest sample time (step_size 0.01 s): the sub-containers exchange their values as often as the fastest FMU. Without step_size, the parent takes the largest step of the sub-containers (0.05 s): the fast FMUs then exchange their values only every 0.05 s.
  • A sub-container slower than its parent steps its FMUs with the inputs of the beginning of each of its steps, and holds its outputs until the end of the step, as Simulink does with a block of a slower sample time (see Communication step and internal step). With the parent at the fastest sample time, every FMU receives at every step the same inputs as in Simulink (single-tasking).

In multi-tasking, Simulink also delays the transfers from a slow block to a fast one by one period of the slow block (deterministic Rate Transition). The container has no such delay.

docs.title: Delays between FMUs
docs.text:
In Simulink, at each step, an FMU block reads its outputs (as computed by its last step), then sets its inputs from the outputs of the blocks upstream and steps. An output that an FMU computes from its inputs therefore reaches the next FMU one step later: along a chain A → B → C where B passes its input to its output, C sees the value of A one step after B does, even when B declares a direct dependency (feedthrough) of this output on its input.

The default scheduling of the container gives the same delays: on such a chain, the inputs received by each FMU at every step are the same as in Simulink. The sequential option steps the FMUs one after the other in the order of the fmu list, each one with the outputs just computed by the previous ones: along the order of the chain, the delays disappear, which changes the results compared to Simulink (the build warns when the order of the fmu list does not follow the links). Keep the default scheduling to reproduce Simulink.

docs.title: Computation time
docs.text: Simulink runs the FMU blocks of one sample time one after the other, even in multi-tasking (one task per rate). The mt option of the container runs each embedded FMU in its own thread: the computation time of FMUs of the same rate is shared between the cores, without changing the results.

docs.title: Validation checklist
docs.text:
1. Same FMU files, same parameter values and start values (including the 0 of the unconnected inputs).
  2. auto_link and auto_input set to false; every Simulink line has its link.
  3. step_size chosen per Sample times; no warning about the step size when the container is built, or warnings understood.
  4. Default scheduling (no sequential).
  5. Same stop time; simulate the container (e.g. with fmpy) with an output interval equal to its step.
  6. Compare the outputs at the common sample times; a difference at the beginning only points at the initialization (an unconnected input, a loop of links), a difference that grows points at the sample times or at a start value.

docs.title: How to Contribute
docs.text: You're welcome to share your ideas or join us in contributing to the project. By getting involved, you help enhance the project and make it accessible to a wider community.

docs.title: Reporting Issues
docs.text:
If you encounter a bug or unexpected behavior, please follow these steps:

  1. Check the existing issues to see if the problem has already been reported.
  2. If not, open a new issue and include:
    • A clear and concise description of the problem.
    • Steps to reproduce the issue, if applicable.
    • Details about your environment (e.g., operating system, Python version).
    • Any relevant error messages or logs.

docs.title: Suggestions for Improvements
docs.text:
We're always happy to hear new ideas for features or enhancements! If you'd like to suggest one:

  1. Check whether someone has already proposed it.
  2. If not, open a new issue describing the improvement and include:
    • A clear explanation of the feature and its use cases.
    • Why it would add value to the project.
    • Examples of how the feature could work, if applicable.

docs.title: Submitting Code
docs.text: For legal reasons, we are unable to accept pull requests. If you have ideas for improvements, please create an issue or get in touch with the development team.

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
The test suite lives under tests/ and uses pytest. It is organised by test type:

Directory Contents tests/unit/ fast, pure-Python tests (model description, operations, checkers, container internals, MCP server) — no FMI simulation tests/integration/ container / split / CLI tests, invariants of the operations, file I/O, optional FMI simulation (fmpy) tests/gui/ PySide6 GUI tests (require pytest-qt) tests/data/<area>/ read-only reference data (FMUs, JSON, CSV, …) per functional area tests/_helpers/ helpers shared by the tests (see below) tests/benchmarks/ performance measurements, not collected by pytest (see below)

docs.title: Install the test dependencies
docs.text:
The tests run against the installed package. From the repository root, install it in editable mode (pip ≥ 21.3):

pip install -e ".[all]"       # full dev setup: GUI, MCP and test dependencies
# or, the test dependencies only:
pip install -e ".[test]"      # pytest, pytest-qt, pytest-cov, fmpy, numpy, PySide6

pip install -r requirements.txt is equivalent to the first command.

docs.title: Run the suite
docs.text:
Tests are run from the tests/ directory (the pytest.ini there sets the import paths):

cd tests
pytest                        # run everything
pytest --cov=fmu_manipulation_toolbox        # with coverage
pytest -v integration/test_container.py      # a single module

docs.title: Selecting a subset with markers
docs.text:
Markers are declared in tests/pytest.ini. Select (or exclude) with -m:

pytest -m unit                # fast unit tests only
pytest -m "not gui"           # skip the GUI tests
pytest -m "integration and fmi3"
pytest -m lsbus               # LS-BUS tests
Marker Meaning unit / integration / gui test type slow end-to-end test running an FMI simulation needs_fmpy requires the fmpy package needs_container / needs_remoting requires the compiled container / remoting binaries windows_only only runs on win32 (auto-skipped elsewhere) fmi2 / fmi3 exercises a specific FMI version lsbus exercises the LS-BUS feature area(name) selects the tests/data/<name> directory copied into tests/tmp/<test>

Platform- or binary-dependent tests are skipped automatically (with an explicit reason) when their prerequisites are missing — they never fail silently.

docs.title: Adding a test
docs.text:
1. Put reference data under tests/data/<area>/ (inputs and REF-* files only — never commit generated outputs). Every FMU of tests/data/ is picked up automatically by integration/test_operations_invariants.py, which checks that each built-in operation keeps an XSD-valid descriptor valid and that read-only operations leave it unchanged.
  2. Add the test to the matching module in tests/unit/, tests/integration/ or tests/gui/.
  3. Decorate it with the relevant markers, e.g. @pytest.mark.area("<area>"). The area_dir fixture copies that data directory into tests/tmp/<test>/ and chdirs into it, so your test can refer to files by their bare names and write outputs without polluting the source tree. The tests/tmp/ tree is wiped at the start of every session and kept afterwards, so the generated artefacts are easy to inspect when debugging a failure.
  4. Reuse the shared helpers in tests/_helpers/:
    • assertions.py: file and XML comparisons (assert_identical_files, assert_equivalent_xml, …);
    • simulation.py: FMI simulation with fmpy and comparison with a reference. Simulate through simulate() rather than fmpy.simulate_fmu(): it always gives a logger to fmpy, whose default logger crashes the process after a simulation given a logger (fmpy 0.3.32);
    • mcp_budget.py: synthetic FMUs and assemblies of industrial size, and the context budget of the MCP server (python tests/_helpers/mcp_budget.py prints its measurements);
    • assistant_bridge.py: FakeBridge, an in-memory bridge to drive the MCP server without Qt.
  5. Write the docstrings and comments of a test about the behaviour it checks and why it matters, not about the plan, the phase or the issue that introduced it: the history belongs to git.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
tests/benchmarks/bench_manipulation.py measures the time and the peak memory of FMU.apply_operation on large synthetic descriptors, to spot a performance regression. It is not part of the test suite; run it from the repository root, it prints a Markdown table:

python tests/benchmarks/bench_manipulation.py [--variables 1000 10000 100000] [--repeat 3]

docs.title: Screenshots of the documentation
docs.text:
The screenshots of the graphical interfaces in the user guide are made by tools/screenshots.py, from the FMUs of tests/data: after a change of an interface, make them again rather than by hand, so that they all look alike. The windows are rendered without being shown, with the native style of the platform (the published ones are made on macOS); PySide6 is needed, and the mcp extra for the AI Assistant entries of the Configuration menu:

python tools/screenshots.py                 # every screenshot, written into docs/
python tools/screenshots.py --list          # their names and files
python tools/screenshots.py fmutool canvas-menu

docs.title: Announcement carousel
docs.text:
The slides announcing version 2.0, shown on the page What's new in 2.0 and posted on LinkedIn, are drawn by tools/make_carousel.py (texts in its SLIDES, images from the documentation and the resources of the package). PySide6 is needed. It writes into one directory the PDF of the LinkedIn post, a PNG preview and the WebP slides of the documentation; copy the WebP files into docs/assets/release-2.0/:

python tools/make_carousel.py --out /tmp/carousel
cp /tmp/carousel/*.webp docs/assets/release-2.0/

The LinkedIn post uses a shorter carousel, sized for LinkedIn: the cover, one slide per main new feature and the call to action, whose QR code points to the documentation (LINKEDIN_SLIDES). --linkedin writes only its PDF and its PNG preview; the QR code needs segno (pip install segno):

python tools/make_carousel.py --linkedin --out /tmp/carousel-linkedin

The banner announcing the page, at the top of the site, is withdrawn by removing the announce block of overrides/main.html; the page stays.

docs.title: Benchmark of the container runtime
docs.text:
tools/bench_container.py measures the runtime of the containers (container/) on reproducible cases, built from the FMUs of tests/data: Co-Simulation FMUs with ports of every type or of one type, Model-Exchange FMUs with and without couplings, Co-Simulation FMUs feeding Model-Exchange ones. fmpy and the runtime built for the host are needed. For each case, it prints the time of the simulation loop (doStep only: the extraction and the instantiation of the container are not timed), the number of FMI calls of the exchanges of one step, and a digest of the results, which must not change when the runtime is optimized:

python tools/bench_container.py                    # every case, 5 runs each
python tools/bench_container.py --list             # their names
python tools/bench_container.py D-mixed --runs 10

Measurements made in separate sessions differ by 5 to 10 %: to compare two versions of the runtime, build the old one in another directory and alternate both container.dylib (.so, .dll) in fmu_manipulation_toolbox/resources/<platform> within one session, keeping the best time of each. The results of reference containers are also compared bit for bit by tests/integration/test_container_perf.py.

docs.title: Packaging and releases
docs.text: The package is described by pyproject.toml (built with setuptools); MANIFEST.in selects the content of the source distribution.

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
The version comes from the git tags, through setuptools-scm: a release tagged V1.9.4.2 is published as 1.9.4.2, and any other commit gets a development version such as 1.9.4.3.dev79+g230faf6. There is no version number to edit in the sources. A clone needs the tags (git fetch --tags) to compute it; a shallow clone gives 0.1.dev1+g<commit>.

Pre-releases use rc tags (V2.0.0rc1). Never use dev tags (V0.0dev3): setuptools-scm cannot compute the version of the later commits from them, and every build fails.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
pip install build
python -m build --sdist --wheel

Build both archives from the source tree: the wheel embeds the prebuilt native binaries of every platform (fmu_manipulation_toolbox/resources/<platform>/, produced by the CI), which the sdist leaves out. A wheel built from the sdist would have no binaries.

docs.title: Content check
docs.text:
tools/dist_inventory.py builds the archives and compares them with the reference of tests/data/packaging/ (data files and binaries of the wheel, metadata, entry points) and with rules computed from the files tracked by git (Python modules of the wheel, content of the sdist). The CI runs it on every build.

pip install build
python tools/dist_inventory.py --check tests/data/packaging                          # needs the binaries
python tools/dist_inventory.py --check tests/data/packaging --placeholder-binaries   # without them

Add --untracked to take files not yet added to git into account. After a deliberate change (new data file, dependency, entry point), review the difference and update the reference:

python tools/dist_inventory.py --write tests/data/packaging --placeholder-binaries

docs.title: Troubleshooting Guide
docs.text: This guide helps you resolve common issues with FMU Manipulation Toolbox.

docs.title: ❌ Command fmutool not found
docs.text:
Symptom: 

'fmutool' is not recognized as an internal or external command

Cause: Python scripts directory is not in PATH.

Solution:

Windows: 

# Find scripts path
python -m site --user-base
# Add %APPDATA%\Python\Python3X\Scripts to your PATH

# Or use directly:
python -m fmu_manipulation_toolbox.fmutool -h

Linux/macOS: 

# Add to PATH in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

# Reload
source ~/.bashrc

docs.title: ❌ Modifications not applied
docs.text:
Symptom: Output FMU is identical to original.

Cause: Missing -output option

Solution: 

# ❌ INCORRECT (no save)
fmutool -input module.fmu -remove-toplevel

# ✅ CORRECT
fmutool -input module.fmu -remove-toplevel -output module-modified.fmu

docs.title: ❌ CSV renaming error
docs.text:
Symptom: 

Error: Port 'xyz' not found in CSV file

Solutions:

  1. Incorrect CSV format
# Generate correct CSV first
fmutool -input module.fmu -dump-csv ports.csv

# Verify format (must contain: name;newName;...)
head ports.csv
  1. File encoding

CSV must be UTF-8 encoded with semicolon (;) separator

  1. Missing names in CSV
# Regenerate complete CSV
fmutool -input module.fmu -dump-csv ports_complete.csv

docs.title: ❌ Name collision after modification
docs.text:
Symptom: 

Error: Duplicate variable name after renaming: 'Temperature'

Cause: Two different variables have the same new name.

Solution:

Check your renaming CSV: 

# ❌ INCORRECT (two variables → same name)
Motor.Temperature;Temperature;0;output;continuous
Controller.Temperature;Temperature;1;output;continuous

# ✅ CORRECT (distinct names)
Motor.Temperature;Motor_Temperature;0;output;continuous
Controller.Temperature;Controller_Temperature;1;output;continuous

docs.title: ❌ GUI won't launch
docs.text:
Symptom: 

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'PySide6'

Solution:

pip install PySide6

docs.title: ❌ FMU Container Builder: wires have no port mappings
docs.text:
Symptom: After loading an existing FMU container, clicking on a wire shows empty mapping tables in both tabs.

Cause: The container FMU may have been built with a version that did not store port-level mappings. Or the .fmu file is corrupted.

Solution:

  1. Select the wire
  2. Click Link Assistant: it opens on Same name and proposes the links between ports of matching names; click Stage checked links, switch the direction (B → A) to do the same, then Apply (see Link Assistant)
  3. Manually adjust if needed using the combo-box dropdowns in each tab

docs.title: ❌ FMU Container fails to instantiate: format version of container.txt
docs.text:
Symptom: the importer cannot instantiate a container FMU, and its log shows: 

Configuration error(...): line #1: container.txt format version 6, this runtime reads version 7: build the container again with the version of FMU Manipulation Toolbox that provides this runtime.
or container.txt has no format version header.

Cause: the resources/container.txt of the container and its runtime (binaries/) come from different versions of FMU Manipulation Toolbox: the file was edited or copied from another container, or the binaries were replaced.

Solution: build the container again (fmucontainer, the Python API or fmucontainer-gui) with one version of FMU Manipulation Toolbox. To rebuild a container whose description is lost, fmusplit extracts the embedded FMUs and a description file from it.

docs.title: ❌ FMU fails to load: missing DLL dependencies
docs.text:
Symptom: a container or a remoted FMU cannot be instantiated, and its log shows DLL ... has missing dependencies. followed by Cannot load ....

Cause: the DLL of the FMU depends on DLLs that are found neither in its directory (binaries/win64 or win32) nor in the system directories or the PATH.

Solution: on Windows, the runtime searches the dependencies of the DLL first in its own directory: add the missing DLLs to the binaries/<platform> directory of the FMU. On Linux and macOS, the dependencies of a shared library are found in its directory only if it is linked with an RPATH set to $ORIGIN (@loader_path on macOS): ask the provider of the FMU for such a build.

docs.title: ❌ FMU Variable Editor: changes are not saved
docs.text:
Symptom: After editing variable names or descriptions, saving the FMU does not apply the changes.

Cause: Only modified cells (highlighted in orange) are written to the output FMU. If no cell appears orange, the edit was not registered.

Solution:

  • Make sure to press Enter or click another cell after editing to confirm the change.
  • Look for the orange highlight on modified cells before saving.

docs.title: ❌ Available GUI commands
docs.text:
All GUI tools can be launched independently:

Command Description fmutoolbox Launcher with all GUI tools fmutool-gui FMU analysis & modification fmueditor FMU variable editor fmucontainer-gui FMU container builder

docs.title: ❌ Operations don't modify the FMU
docs.text:
Wrong code: 

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU, OperationStripTopLevel

fmu = FMU("module.fmu")
operation = OperationStripTopLevel()
# ❌ Operation not applied!
fmu.repack("output.fmu")

Correct code: 

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU, OperationStripTopLevel

fmu = FMU("module.fmu")
operation = OperationStripTopLevel()
fmu.apply_operation(operation)  # ✅ Apply the operation!
fmu.repack("output.fmu")

docs.title: Need More Help?
docs.text:
1. Check the complete documentation
  2. Search GitHub Issues
  3. Create a new issue with system details and error message

Last updated: April 2026

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide will get you up and running with FMU Manipulation Toolbox in less than 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin, ensure you have:

  • Python 3.10 or higher
  • pip (Python package manager)
  • An FMU file to work with (or use our examples)

What is an FMU?

A Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU) is a standardized format for model exchange and co-simulation defined by the FMI Standard. FMUs are widely used in automotive, aerospace, and industrial automation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install FMU Manipulation Toolbox using pip:

pip install fmu-manipulation-toolbox

Verify the installation:

fmutool --help
Installation successful!

You should see the help message displaying all available commands. If you encounter issues, check our Troubleshooting Guide.

docs.title: Your First FMU Analysis
docs.text: Let's start by analyzing an existing FMU to understand its structure.

docs.title: Step 1: Get FMU Information
docs.text:
Command LinePython APIGraphical Interface 
fmutool -input my_model.fmu -summary

Expected Output: 

FMU Information:
  Name: my_module
  FMI Version: 2.0
  GUID: {12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789012}
  Number of variables: 42
  Number of parameters: 5
  Number of inputs: 8
  Number of outputs: 12


from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU, OperationSummary
from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.cli.utils import setup_logger

setup_logger()

# Load the FMU
fmu = FMU("my_model.fmu")

# Display summary using logging facilities
fmu.apply_operation(OperationSummary())

Requires the gui extra

fmutool-gui needs PySide6, installed via pip install "fmu-manipulation-toolbox[gui]" — see the Installation Guide.

fmutool-gui
  1. Click (or drag & drop your FMU onto) the drop zone
  2. Select your FMU file
  3. View the summary in the log area

docs.title: Step 2: List All Ports
docs.text:
Export all port information to a CSV file for easy viewing:

fmutool -input my_module.fmu -dump-csv ports_list.csv

Open ports_list.csv to see all ports with their attributes:

name causality variability type valueReference Motor.Temperature output continuous Real 0 Motor.Speed input continuous Real 1 Controller.Gain parameter fixed Real 2

Pro Tip: Excel Integration

Open the CSV in Excel or LibreOffice Calc for easy filtering and sorting. Use semicolon (;) as the delimiter.

docs.title: Your First FMU Modification
docs.text: Now let's modify an FMU by simplifying its port hierarchy.

docs.title: Problem: Complex Hierarchy
docs.text:
Your FMU has this structure:

System.Motor.Temperature
System.Motor.Speed
System.Controller.Gain

You want to simplify it to:

Motor.Temperature
Motor.Speed
Controller.Gain

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Command LinePython APIGraphical Interface 
fmutool -input my_module.fmu \
  -remove-toplevel \
  -output my_module_simplified.fmu

Verify the result:

fmutool -input my_module_simplified.fmu -summary

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU, OperationStripTopLevel

# Load FMU
fmu = FMU("my_module.fmu")

# Apply transformation
operation = OperationStripTopLevel()
fmu.apply_operation(operation)

# Save result
fmu.repack("my_module_simplified.fmu")

(requires the gui extra — see Step 1)

  1. Load your FMU
  2. Click Remove Toplevel
  3. Click Save modified FMU as and choose output filename

Important: Original FMU Preservation

The original FMU is never modified. All operations create a new copy, ensuring data safety.

docs.title: Batch Renaming with CSV
docs.text: For complex renaming operations, use CSV files.

docs.title: Step 1: Generate Renaming Template
docs.text: fmutool -input my_module.fmu -dump-csv renaming.csv

docs.title: Step 2: Edit the CSV
docs.text:
Open renaming.csv and modify the newName column:

Before: 

name;newName;valueReference;causality;variability
Motor.Temp;Motor.Temp;0;output;continuous
Motor.RPM;Motor.RPM;1;input;continuous

After: 

name;newName;valueReference;causality;variability
Motor.Temp;Engine_Temperature;0;output;continuous
Motor.RPM;Rotation_Speed;1;input;continuous

Empty newName = Port Removal

Leave newName empty to remove a port from the FMU.

docs.title: Step 3: Apply Renaming
docs.text:
fmutool -input my_module.fmu \
  -rename-from-csv renaming.csv \
  -output my_module_renamed.fmu

docs.title: Common Operations
docs.text:
Here are the most frequently used operations:

  • Filter Ports

    Keep only ports matching a pattern:

    fmutool -input module.fmu \
  -keep-only-regexp "^Motor\..*" \
  -output module_motor.fmu

  • Remove Internals

    Remove all internal variables:

    fmutool -input module.fmu \
  -remove-regexp "^Internal\..*" \
  -output module_clean.fmu

  • Validate FMU

    Check FMI compliance:

    fmutool -input module.fmu -check

  • Extract Parameters

    List only parameters:

    fmutool -input module.fmu \
  -only-parameters \
  -dump-csv parameters.csv

docs.title: Your First FMU Container
docs.text: An FMU Container is a standard FMU that embeds other FMUs inside it. This is useful to combine multiple models into a single simulation unit, letting your FMI tool orchestrate a complex assembly as if it were a single FMU.

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
Imagine you have two FMUs modeling a bouncing ball:

  • bb_position.fmu — computes the ball position
  • bb_velocity.fmu — computes the ball velocity

These two FMUs need to exchange data: velocity feeds into position, and a ground-detection signal feeds back. Instead of wiring them manually in your simulation tool, you can package them together as a single FMU Container.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Description File
docs.text:
The easiest way is to use a CSV file describing which FMUs to include and how to connect them.

Create a file container.csv:

rule;from_fmu;from_port;to_fmu;to_port
FMU;bb_position.fmu;;;
FMU;bb_velocity.fmu;;;
OUTPUT;bb_position.fmu;position1;;position
LINK;bb_position.fmu;is_ground;bb_velocity.fmu;reset
LINK;bb_velocity.fmu;velocity;bb_position.fmu;velocity
OUTPUT;bb_velocity.fmu;velocity;;

Here's what each rule means:

Rule Meaning FMU Declare an embedded FMU OUTPUT Expose a port from an embedded FMU as a container output LINK Connect an output of one embedded FMU to an input of another

Auto-wiring

By default, fmucontainer will automatically connect ports with matching names (auto_link) and expose unconnected inputs/outputs (auto_input, auto_output). You only need to declare explicit connections for ports with different names.

docs.title: Step 2: Build the Container
docs.text:
Command LineWith OptionsJSON Format

Place your FMUs and the CSV file in the same directory, then run:

fmucontainer -container container.csv:0.1

The :0.1 suffix sets the container's internal time step to 0.1 seconds.

The resulting container.fmu is ready to use in any FMI-compatible tool.

You can customize the container creation:

# FMUs are in a specific directory
fmucontainer -container container.csv:0.1 -fmu-directory ./my_fmus

# Enable multi-threading for parallel execution
fmucontainer -container container.csv:0.1 -mt

# Generate an FMI 3.0 container
fmucontainer -container container.csv:0.1 -fmi 3

For more control, use a JSON description file instead of CSV:

{
  "name": "bouncing.fmu",
  "mt": true,
  "profiling": false,
  "auto_link": true,
  "auto_input": true,
  "auto_output": true,
  "fmu": [
    "bb_position.fmu",
    "bb_velocity.fmu"
  ],
  "output": [
    ["bb_position.fmu", "position1", "position"],
    ["bb_velocity.fmu", "velocity", "velocity"]
  ],
  "link": [
    ["bb_position.fmu", "is_ground", "bb_velocity.fmu", "reset"],
    ["bb_velocity.fmu", "velocity", "bb_position.fmu", "velocity"]
  ]
}

Then build with:

fmucontainer -container bouncing.json

docs.title: Step 3: Verify the Result
docs.text:
Use fmutool to inspect the generated container just like any other FMU:

fmutool -input container.fmu -summary

Learn More

FMU Containers support advanced features like profiling, variable step sizes, and LS-BUS routing. See the full Container documentation for details.

docs.title: Essential Commands Reference
docs.text: Command Description -summary Display FMU information -check Validate FMI compliance -dump-csv file.csv Export ports to CSV -remove-toplevel Remove top hierarchy level -rename-from-csv file.csv Batch rename from CSV -keep-only-regexp "pattern" Keep matching ports only -remove-regexp "pattern" Remove matching ports

docs.title: Quick Troubleshooting
docs.text:
FMU Won't Load

Check the FMU validity: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -check

Common causes: - Corrupted ZIP archive - Invalid modelDescription.xml - Missing required files

Modifications Not Applied

Did you forget the -output option?

❌ Wrong: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -remove-toplevel

✅ Correct: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -remove-toplevel -output module_flat.fmu

CSV Renaming Error

Ensure your CSV file:

  • Is UTF-8 encoded
  • Uses semicolon (;) as delimiter
  • Contains all required columns: name;newName;...
  • Includes all ports from the original FMU

docs.text:
Now that you've mastered the basics, explore more advanced features:

  • CLI Guide

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: This section provides in-depth documentation for every feature of FMU Manipulation Toolbox. Whether you prefer a graphical interface, the command line, or a Python script, you'll find guidance here.

docs.title: Features at a Glance
docs.text:
FMU Manipulation Toolbox offers five main capabilities:

  • Analysis

    Inspect FMU contents, list ports, validate against XSD schemas, and run compliance checks.

    CLI Reference · Python API · GUI

  • Modification

    Rename ports, filter variables, strip hierarchy levels, and batch-edit attributes — all without recompilation.

    CLI Reference · Python API · GUI

  • FMU Containers

    Combine multiple FMUs into a single container with automatic or explicit routing, multi-threading, and profiling.

    CLI Reference · Python API · GUI

  • Remoting

    Add cross-bitness interfaces (32 ↔ 64-bit) or run an FMU in a separate process via a frontend wrapper.

    Remoting Guide · CLI Reference · GUI

  • Checker

    Validate FMUs against built-in rules or your own custom checkers.

    Checker Guide

docs.title: Available Interfaces
docs.text:
All features are accessible through the Command Line Interface and the Python API. The Graphical User Interface supports a subset of operations, as summarized below:

Feature CLI Python API GUI Analysis Modification FMU Variable Editor — — FMU Containers Remoting Checker

Which interface should I use?

  • GUI — Best for interactive exploration: loading an FMU, visually inspecting its ports, applying quick modifications, editing variables, or building FMU containers with a node-graph editor. The Launcher gives you quick access to all GUI tools.
  • CLI — Ideal for automation, scripting, and CI/CD pipelines. Every feature is available from the command line.
  • Python API — Offers full programmatic control for complex workflows, batch processing, and custom integrations.

docs.title: Launcher
docs.text: Guide Description FMU Toolbox Launcher Unified entry point for all GUI tools (fmutoolbox)

docs.title: Understand & Modify FMUs
docs.text: Guide Description CLI Usage Complete reference for all fmutool command-line options Operations GUI Step-by-step guide to the graphical interface (fmutool-gui) Variable Editor Spreadsheet-like editor for variable names, descriptions, and experiment settings (fmueditor) Python API Programmatic access to analysis and modification operations Remoting Add cross-bitness or frontend interfaces to your FMUs Checker Built-in and custom FMU validation rules

docs.title: FMU Container
docs.text: Guide Description Container Concept How to combine multiple FMUs into a single container Container Builder Visual node-graph editor to build containers (fmucontainer-gui) Variable Step Size Handling variable step sizes inside containers Datalog Logging simulation data from containers LS-BUS Support Network bus signal routing in containers

docs.title: FMU Toolbox Launcher
docs.text: The FMU Toolbox Launcher is the unified entry point for all graphical tools provided by FMU Manipulation Toolbox. It presents a home screen with quick-access buttons to each GUI application.

docs.title: Launching
docs.text: fmutoolbox

docs.title: Available Tools
docs.text:
The launcher window offers three buttons:

Button Tool Command Description Operations on FMU FMU Tool GUI fmutool-gui Analyze and modify FMUs: rename ports, remove variables, add remoting, check compliance, etc. FMU Variables Editor FMU Variable Editor fmueditor Spreadsheet-like editor to rename variables, edit descriptions, and adjust experiment settings. FMU Container Build FMU Container Builder fmucontainer-gui Visual node-graph editor to assemble multiple FMUs into a container.

Each button opens the corresponding tool in a separate window. You can have multiple tools open at the same time.

Each window has its own log: the messages of an action (loading an FMU, an operation, a build, the AI Assistant of a Container Builder) are only shown in the window where it runs. The few messages that do not come from a window are shown in all the open windows.

Direct launch

You can also launch each tool individually from the command line without going through the launcher. See the table above for the corresponding commands.

docs.title: AI Assistant (MCP server)
docs.text:
The toolbox exposes its FMU Container assembly capabilities to an AI agent (such as GitHub Copilot in Agent mode) through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

It comes in two flavours, serving exactly the same tools:

Flavour How it starts What the agent drives GUI AI Assistant On in the Container Builder The live canvas Standalone fmutool-mcp, launched by the MCP client An in-memory assembly

With the GUI flavour, FMUs the agent adds, links it creates and options it sets appear immediately in the window. Every action is marked as an unsaved change (so it can be reviewed, undone or saved) and is written to the log as an [AI] … message: the last one is shown in the status bar, and all of them in the log window (click the status bar).

The standalone flavour needs neither a display nor a running GUI, and speaks the stdio transport that most MCP clients expect from a server they launch themselves. Nothing is visible until the agent exports or builds the assembly.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• The optional fastmcp package. It is not installed by default: pull it in through the mcp extra of the toolbox:
pip install "fmu-manipulation-toolbox[mcp]"

To combine it with the GUI (required to run the Container Builder), use:

pip install "fmu-manipulation-toolbox[gui,mcp]"

docs.title: Starting the standalone server
docs.text:
The server is normally launched by the MCP client, not by hand. Declare it as a command (see Connecting a client that launches the server below); the useful options are:

fmutool-mcp [--transport stdio|http] [--root DIR] [--host H] [--port P] [--name container.fmu] [--token TOKEN]
  • --transport stdio (the default) is what a client that spawns the server expects. --transport http lets clients attach to an already-running server instead.
  • --root DIR confines the assistant to a directory tree. Use it: it is what keeps an agent from reading or writing anywhere on your disk. The FMUCONTAINER_MCP_ROOT environment variable does the same.
  • --token generate requires a bearer token from HTTP clients and prints it. See Security; it is pointless with the stdio transport.

All logs go to stderr, since with the stdio transport stdout carries the protocol itself.

docs.title: Starting the server from the GUI
docs.text:
1. Launch the Container Builder (fmucontainer-gui).
  2. Open the Configuration menu (bottom-left button).
  3. Select AI Assistant On.

The server listens locally using the Streamable HTTP transport on:

http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp

The port can be overridden with the FMUCONTAINER_MCP_PORT environment variable. The server is bound to 127.0.0.1 only.

Once the server really listens, the log window shows AI Assistant enabled — connect your MCP client to http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp. If it cannot start (port already taken, for instance), an error is shown instead and the menu switches back to AI Assistant Off.

docs.title: Tuning the timeout
docs.text:
Each tool waits for the GUI to apply its operation before answering (this concerns the GUI flavour only — the standalone server has no window to wait for). That budget defaults to 60 s and can be changed with FMUCONTAINER_MCP_TIMEOUT (a number of seconds):

FMUCONTAINER_MCP_TIMEOUT=180 fmucontainer-gui

Building a container may be slower than editing one, so save_as_json and save_as_fmu get ten times that budget automatically — there is no second variable to set.

A timeout means the window did not answer, usually because a dialog is waiting for you; it does not mean the operation failed. Check the window before retrying.

Select AI Assistant Off (or close the window) to stop the server.

docs.title: Connecting a client that launches the server
docs.text:
This is the standalone flavour: the client spawns fmutool-mcp itself, so there is nothing to start beforehand.

Claude Desktop — add to claude_desktop_config.json (~/Library/Application Support/Claude/ on macOS, %APPDATA%\Claude\ on Windows):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "fmutool": {
      "command": "fmutool-mcp",
      "args": ["--root", "/path/to/my/fmus"]
    }
  }
}

VS Code — in .vscode/mcp.json:

{
  "servers": {
    "fmutool": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "fmutool-mcp",
      "args": ["--root", "${workspaceFolder}"]
    }
  }
}

The fmutool key is the name the client will show you; it is yours to choose, and does not have to match the name the server advertises.

If fmutool-mcp is not on the PATH of the client (a common case when the toolbox lives in a virtual environment), give the absolute path of the script, or use "command": "/path/to/venv/bin/python" with "args": ["-m", "fmu_manipulation_toolbox.cli.fmutool_mcp", ...].

docs.title: Connecting GitHub Copilot to the GUI server
docs.text: Copilot must be in Agent mode (MCP servers are not used in Ask mode), and the server must be started before Copilot connects.

docs.title: JetBrains IDEs
docs.text:
Open the Copilot chat, switch to Agent mode, open the tools/settings menu and Edit MCP configuration (Settings → Languages & Frameworks → GitHub Copilot → Model Context Protocol), then add:

{
  "servers": {
    "fmutool": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Create .vscode/mcp.json at the root of your workspace:

{
  "servers": {
    "fmutool": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Available tools
docs.text: Tool Description list_fmus List FMUs currently in the assembly list_fmu_ports List the ports of an FMU on the canvas, with filters and paging inspect_fmu_file Describe an .fmu file without adding it to the assembly add_fmu Add an FMU file to the assembly; adding a file again adds another instance of it (model-1.fmu), whose name is returned remove_fmu Remove an FMU and its wires add_link / add_links Connect an output port to an input port, one at a time or in bulk remove_link Disconnect an explicit link expose_input / expose_output Surface a port on the container boundary set_start_value / unset_start_value Set, or drop, a start value / parameter set_container_options Set step_size, mt, profiling, auto_*, … get_assembly_json Review the assembly; a large one comes one container, then one section, at a time analyze_assembly Summarise the assembly, or lint it before building (see Analysing an assembly) save_as_json Export the assembly description save_as_fmu Build the container FMU (FMI 2 or 3), reporting progress

docs.title: Single-FMU tools
docs.text:
These come from fmutool and the Checker. They read or rewrite one .fmu file and never touch the assembly:

Tool Description summarize_fmu Identity, capabilities, platforms, embedded resources, port counts check_fmu Conformity to the FMI standard: schema and semantic rules, plus any registered checker dump_ports_csv Export every port to a CSV file, for bulk renaming rename_ports_from_csv Rename — or drop — ports from that CSV apply_operation Strip/merge a Bus. prefix, trim, or filter ports by regexp

The three that rewrite an FMU always produce a new file and leave the source untouched. They change the FMU interface, so anything already connected to the old port names will break.

check_fmu answers compliant: true only when the descriptor validates against the FMI schema and no checker reports an error (compliant_with gives the FMI version of the schema). To keep the answer small, the messages of the same rule are grouped, with their count and a few examples — 2500 variables without start value make one entry — and at most 50 groups are returned per list; error_count and warning_count give the totals and truncated tells whether groups were left out. The full report is printed by fmutool -input model.fmu -check.

An empty newName removes the port

In the CSV consumed by rename_ports_from_csv, a row whose second column is empty deletes that port. The tool reports renamed and removed separately so the assistant can tell you what actually happened.

docs.title: Reading port listings
docs.text:
list_fmu_ports and inspect_fmu_file report every variable of the FMU — inputs, outputs, parameters and locals alike — each with its causality, variability, type, unit, start value and description. Attributes the FMU does not declare are left out, and descriptions are cut after 80 characters.

Industrial FMUs have thousands of variables, so the answer is bounded: 50 ports are returned per call by default, at most 200 with limit. Rather than paging blindly, narrow the request:

  • causality=["output"] before looking for something to wire,
  • name_pattern="^engine_" to search by name (a regular expression),
  • offset to fetch the next page when truncated is true.

The counts field always describes the whole FMU, whatever the filter, and total counts the ports matching the filter. Comparing returned with total tells the assistant whether it has seen everything.

Two resources are also exposed: guide://usage (how to drive the tool) and assembly://current (the current assembly as JSON).

docs.title: Reading the assembly
docs.text:
get_assembly_json returns the assembly in the format of a JSON description, the FMUs being designated by their name, as in the other tools (save_as_json still writes the complete file). A real assembly of a few hundred ports is over 100,000 characters, far more than a tool answer can carry, so the answer is bounded:

  • a small assembly is returned whole;
  • otherwise, one container at a time: the root by default, any other one with node="sub.fmu" (its name). The answer gives its options, its FMUs, the counts of its sections, and its sub-containers reduced to their name and counts;
  • when even one container is too large, its sections are left out and truncated is true: read them with section (input, output, link, start or drop), 50 entries per call by default, 200 at most with limit, the next ones with offset.

assembly://current follows the same rule, without the arguments.

docs.title: Analysing an assembly
docs.text:
analyze_assembly reads the assembly without building it. Nested containers loaded in the Container Builder are analysed too.

mode="summary" (the default) describes the assembly, container by container: name, options (step_size, mt, auto_*...), FMUs, counts, and the exposed ports and the links grouped by FMU and name prefix — the part before the first ., or before the first _ (Sc_2_DV.speed → Sc_2_DV, SNR_time3 → SNR_) —, each group with its count and a few examples. The ports sharing their prefix with no other port are counted under ungrouped. At most 15 groups are listed per list, the largest first. When the whole tree does not fit, the sub-containers are only given with their name, options, FMUs and counts (reduced): ask for one with node="sub.fmu".

mode="lint" reports the known traps, grouped by rule like the report of check_fmu: error_count, warning_count, info_count, then one group per rule with what the rule means, its count and a few examples naming their container. node="sub.fmu" restricts it to one container.

Rule Severity Meaning input-fed-twice error An input is fed more than once (links and/or exposed inputs) duplicate-output error Several ports exposed under one container output name invalid-input, invalid-output, invalid-link, invalid-drop, invalid-start error An entry refused by the container builder: unknown port, causality, type without conversion, malformed start value... auto-rules-error error An auto_* rule fails at build time, e.g. two outputs auto-exposed under one name nested-mt warning mt enabled on a container and on one of its ancestors mt-sequential warning mt and sequential both enabled step-ratio info / warning The step of a sub-container differs from the step of its container; a warning above a ratio of 10, or when the ratio is not an integer auto-off-nothing-exposed warning auto_input or auto_output off, and nothing of that kind exposed by the root container lossy-link warning A link converts its value with a possible loss of information link-unit warning Linked ports declare different units: the toolbox does not convert them dangling-input warning An input neither linked nor exposed, even by the auto_* rules, and without start value fan-out info One output, or one container input, feeds several inputs source-fmu info Nothing feeds an FMU: a scenario, a stub of constants... (only when auto_link and auto_input are off) auto-rules-partial, sub-container-unchecked, not-checked info What the lint could not check (see below)

The errors are exactly what the container build refuses. The port-level rules are not re-implemented: the assembly is replayed, container by container, into the container builder without building it, so the lint cannot disagree with the build. This needs the FMU files: an FMU the server cannot read is reported as not-checked. On large FMUs, the lint takes a second or two.

A sub-container only exists once built. The entries that involve one (a link to a sub-container, a port it exposes) are therefore not checked against its ports (sub-container-unchecked), and the dry run of the auto_* rules does not see its ports (auto-rules-partial). The lint only reads the description of the assembly: it says nothing of the simulation results.

docs.title: Local models
docs.text:
The tools also work with models run locally, e.g. Qwen, Llama or Mistral served by Ollama or LM Studio, provided their context window is large enough. The definitions of the tools alone take about 4,400 tokens, sent with every request, and every tool result stays in the conversation: a page of ports is about 2,000 tokens.

  • Use a context of 16k tokens at least, 32k recommended. Local runtimes often start with a much smaller one: in Ollama, raise num_ctx (e.g. PARAMETER num_ctx 32768 in a Modelfile, or the options of the API request); in LM Studio, raise the Context Length of the model.
  • When the context is too small, the runtime silently drops the beginning of the conversation: the assistant forgets its tools or its instructions, calls tools that do not exist, or answers without using them. Increase the context, or start a new conversation.
  • Keep the requests narrow: filter the port listings (causality, name_pattern) rather than paging through a whole FMU, and start with analyze_assembly rather than reading a large assembly section by section.

docs.title: Prompts and reference resources
docs.text:
The know-how travels with the server rather than with this repository, so it reaches any MCP client — not only the ones able to read a SKILL.md.

Four prompts describe a complete procedure. They appear in the client as slash-commands or ready-made conversations, and all their arguments are optional:

Prompt Use it when the user… build_container …wants to combine, merge or package several FMUs diagnose_assembly …reports a container that fails to build or misbehaves inspect_fmu …asks what an FMU contains analyze_assembly …asks what the loaded assembly contains and how it works

Four fixed resources and one templated resource carry the reference material:

Resource Content guide://usage The recommended workflow, end to end fmi://conventions Causality, variability, types, units — and their traps container://options Every container option, derived from the tool schema assembly://current The current assembly, as JSON, bounded like get_assembly_json fmu://{name}/ports The ports of one FMU of the assembly, as JSON

container://options is generated from the very model that validates set_container_options, so the documented options can never drift away from the accepted ones.

docs.title: What the assistant can do
docs.text:
The tools act on your behalf: they read .fmu files, and they write .json, .csv and .fmu files wherever you allow them to. Two guard-rails are always on:

  • the destination extension must match the tool (.fmu for a container, .json for a description, .csv for a port dump);
  • an existing file is never replaced unless the caller passes overwrite=True — which an assistant should confirm with you first.

Set FMUCONTAINER_MCP_ROOT (or --root DIR) to confine every read and write to one directory tree. This is the single most useful setting when an agent drives the server.

docs.title: Transport
The client cannot connect
docs.text:
First check, in the log window, that the server announced its address (see Starting the server from the GUI), and that the client is configured with that exact URL. Then test the server without the client:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"test","version":"1"}}}'

On Windows, use curl.exe in cmd, with double quotes around the JSON and its inner quotes escaped (\"). An answer starting with event: message means the server works: the problem is between the client and the server.

docs.title: HTTP proxy of the IDE
docs.text:
An IDE configured with an HTTP proxy may route the requests of its MCP client through that proxy, including the requests to 127.0.0.1. The proxy cannot reach your local server: the client then reports errors such as fetch failed or SSE error: Non-200 status code (400), and the Container Builder log shows no tool call.

Exclude the local addresses from the proxy. In JetBrains IDEs: Settings → Appearance & Behavior → System Settings → HTTP Proxy, add localhost, 127.0.0.1 to No proxy for. Elsewhere, set the NO_PROXY environment variable to localhost,127.0.0.1 before starting the IDE.

docs.title: localhost instead of 127.0.0.1
docs.text: The server listens on the IPv4 address 127.0.0.1 only. Some clients, especially on Windows, resolve localhost to the IPv6 address ::1 first, where the server does not listen (and where another program may answer). Use http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp in the client configuration.

docs.title: Warnings in the console
docs.text:
WARNING:  Unsupported upgrade request.
WARNING:  Invalid HTTP request received.

These come from uvicorn, the HTTP server, when a client tries HTTP/2 or HTTPS first: the server only speaks plain HTTP/1.1 and the client falls back to it. They are harmless as long as the tools work.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• No nested containers can be created. The tools add FMUs to a single, flat container. Use the Container Builder GUI or a hand-written JSON description for a hierarchy. A nested assembly loaded in the GUI can be read and analysed (node); the standalone server only knows flat ones.
  • The lint does not see the ports of sub-containers: the entries that involve a sub-container are not checked against its ports, which only exist once built.
  • No read_assembly. An existing .json description cannot be loaded into the assistant; open it in the GUI instead.
  • auto_link links cannot be removed one by one: they are derived when the container is built. Disable the option and wire explicitly.
  • Units are not converted. Linking m/s to km/h is accepted and gives wrong results; the assistant is told to check, but cannot enforce it.

docs.title: Reset of Embedded FMUs
