docs.text: During a simulation, an embedded FMU sometimes has to start again from its initial state: a controller re-armed by a supervisor, a component replaced on a test bench, a scenario restarted by an event... With the option reset_ports, an FMU of the container (or the importer) can request the reset of another embedded FMU.

docs.title: Principle
docs.text:
With reset_ports, each embedded FMU (sub-containers included) gets a reserved Boolean input, container.reset (fmi2Boolean in an FMI-2 container, fmi3Boolean in an FMI-3 container). This input is not a variable of the FMU: the container reads it.

When it is true at the start of an internal step of the container, the container:

  1. writes a row in the datalog, if any;
  2. resets the FMU (fmi2Reset / fmi3Reset);
  3. initializes it again at the current time of the container: start values, values set by the importer on its exposed inputs and parameters, current values of its inputs, then the event iteration;
  4. runs the step;
  5. writes false into the input at the end of the step.

The input is fed like any input of an embedded FMU:

  • by a link from an output of another FMU (or of the same FMU);
  • or exposed as an input of the container, named container.<fmu>.reset (<fmu>: name of the FMU, lowercase, without .fmu), by auto_input or by an explicit input rule.

A port neither linked nor exposed is reported by a warning at build time: the FMU is never reset.

A pulse, not a level

The input goes back to false at the end of the step that reset the FMU, whoever set it to true. An FMU that keeps its output true resets the target every other step: to reset it once, the source must emit a pulse (true during one step).

docs.title: Same behavior in every mode
docs.text:
The reset is applied at the start of the next internal step, between two steps, in every execution mode (parallel, multi-threaded, sequential): a request made by an FMU during the step n resets the target before the step n+1. One link or one container input may reset several FMUs at once.

Co-Simulation and Model-Exchange FMUs are supported: the solver reads the states of a reset Model-Exchange FMU again. A sub-container is reset with all its FMUs.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Command lineJSONCSVPython 
fmucontainer -container assembly.json -reset-ports

With the default auto_input, every reset input is exposed by the container.

{
  "name": "resettable.fmu",
  "reset_ports": true,
  "fmu": ["supervisor.fmu", "controller.fmu"],
  "link": [["supervisor.fmu", "restart", "controller.fmu", "container.reset"]]
}

An exposed reset input is an input rule: ["container.controller.reset", "controller.fmu", "container.reset"].

The option is given by the command line (-reset-ports); the link is a regular LINK rule:

LINK;supervisor.fmu;restart;controller.fmu;container.reset

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.container import FMUContainer

container = FMUContainer("resettable", "fmus", reset_ports=True)
container.get_fmu("supervisor.fmu")
container.get_fmu("controller.fmu")
container.add_link("supervisor.fmu", "restart", "controller.fmu", "container.reset")
container.add_input("", "supervisor.fmu", "container.reset")    # exposed as container.supervisor.reset
container.make_fmu("resettable.fmu")

reset_ports is a parameter of the constructor: the ports exist as soon as the FMUs are loaded.

The source may be of any type that converts to a Boolean (e.g. a Real is true when it is not 0), as for any link. A start value cannot be set on container.reset.

docs.title: Container Builder
docs.text: In the FMU Container Builder, check reset_ports in the Container Details panel (the root container included): the configuration node gets one <fmu>.reset port per FMU, or sub-container, of that container. Wire an FMU to it, and select the node to expose reset ports as inputs of the container.

docs.title: The container itself
docs.text: fmi2Reset / fmi3Reset of a container are supported: every embedded FMU is reset, and the container goes back to its state after instantiation (its datalog goes on in the same file).

docs.title: Datalog
docs.text:
The datalog writes one row just before the reset, at the same time as the row of the previous step:

  • for an exposed input, its value is 1 in this row only;
  • for a link, the datalog shows the link variable, i.e. the value of the source before its conversion to a Boolean: the reset is visible by the repeated time.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• container.reset is a reserved name: an FMU with a real port of this name cannot be embedded with reset_ports (the build stops with an error). A real port named reset is not concerned.

  • Exposed without explicit name (auto_input, or an input rule with an empty name), the reset input is named container.<fmu>.reset: the build stops with an error if the container already has a variable of this name (e.g. an input of a sub-container): give the input another name explicitly. An explicit name may feed several reset ports, to reset several FMUs at once.

  • The reset of an FMU whose clocks are scheduled by the container (LS-BUS, countdown clocks) is not supported: the step fails with an error.

  • The embedded FMU must support fmi2Reset / fmi3Reset, and an initialization at a start time other than the start of the simulation: if the reset fails, the step fails with an error.
  • fmusplit restores the option reset_ports only when at least one reset input is linked or exposed: without it, nothing in the container tells the option (which then has no effect on the simulation).

docs.title: Container with TS_MULTIPLIER
docs.text:
Sometimes, during the simulation, speed is more important than accuracy. In such case, having a bigger step size could drastically improve performance.

In this very simple test case, we consider two functional units represented as FMUs. 1. The first FMU, VanDerPol, generates two output signals and operates with a variable time step. 2. The second FMU, sched2, produces an integer output defined as follows:

- value 1 for 0 ≤ _t_ < 5,
- value 5 for 5 ≤ _t_ < 15,
- value 1 for 15 ≤ _t_ < 20.

The objective of this study is to use the output of sched2 to dynamically scale the sampling step of the VanDerPol FMU, whose default value is 0.1.

The same assembly can be built visually with the FMU Container Builder GUI, using the configuration node to wire sched2's output to VanDerPol's ts_multiplier input:

The configuration node

The configuration node automatically appears on the canvas as soon as a sub-container — here, nested (containing VanDerPol) — has its ts_multiplier parameter checked. Checking ts_multiplier on the root container would have no effect.

For illustration purposes, you can find the JSON file used to construct this co-simulation setup, along with the corresponding output figure.

docs.title: FMU Containers
docs.text:
An FMU Container is a classical FMU which embeds other FMU's:

From API point of view, an FMUContainer can be seen as * an FMU which implements the FMI API (either version 2.0 or 3.0) * an fmi-importer which can load FMUs

FMU Manipulation Toolbox is shipped with fmucontainer command which makes it easy to nest FMU's into FMU.

Video Presentation

A video presentation of FMU Containers is available on YouTube: FMU Container Presentation

docs.title: How to create an FMU Container ?
docs.text:
The fmucontainer command creates a FMU, named Container, from a description file. This file contains multiple parameters:

  • time_step: a FMU Container acts as a fixed step time "solver" for its embedded FMU's. For Model-Exchange FMU's, this time step is also used as the integration step of the built-in solver. When it is not given, it is deduced from the embedded FMU's (see Default time step).
  • optional features
  • multi-threading: each embedded FMU will use its own thread to parallelize doStep() operation.
  • profiling: performance indicators can be calculated by the container to help to identify the bottlenecks among the embedded FMU's.
  • reset_ports: each embedded FMU gets a container.reset input; when it is true, the container resets the FMU during the simulation (see Reset of Embedded FMUs).
  • routing table
  • Input ports: the list of the Container's inputs. Each input is linked to one input (or more) of one of the embedded FMU's.
  • Output ports: the list of the container's outputs. Each output is linked to one output of one of the embedded FMU's.
  • Connections between embedded FMU's. When the types differ, the value is converted (lossy conversions, such as Float64 to Float32 or a number to a boolean, are reported by a warning).

Each input of an embedded FMU is fed by one source: a container input or a connection, not both, and not two connections. An output can be exposed and connected at the same time. Every port named in the routing table must exist: an unknown FMU or port stops the build with an error. - Explicitly ignored ports (only port with causality = "output" can be ignored) - Automation of routing table - auto_input exposes automatically the (unconnected) ports of embedded FMU's with causality = "input" - auto_output expose automatically the (unconnected) ports of embedded FMU's with causality = "output" - auto_local expose automatically the ports of embedded FMU's with causality = "local" - auto_parameter expose automatically the ports of embedded FMU's with causality = "parameter" - auto_link links automatically ports of embedded FMU's which are left previously unconnected and have the same names and types. The instances of an FMU are never auto-linked: they share the port names of the FMU, so an output would feed the inputs of every instance.

When auto_input or auto_output exposes a port whose name is already used by an input or an output of the container, the port is exposed as <fmu>.<port> instead (e.g. bb_position-1.position1), so that every variable of the container keeps a distinct name.

Some of these parameters can be defined by Command Line Interface or by the input files.

To rebuild as a container an assembly of FMUs made in Simulink, see From Simulink to an FMU Container.

docs.title: Default time step
docs.text:
When no time step is given, the container deduces it from the stepSize of the embedded FMU's (<DefaultExperiment> of their modelDescription.xml):

  • the FMU's which cannot handle a variable communication step size impose their step: the container step is their least common multiple, computed exactly (0.1 and 0.25 give 0.5, 0.2 and 0.3 give 0.6);
  • if all FMU's handle a variable step size, the container step is the largest of their step sizes;
  • FMU's without stepSize are ignored; if none declares one, the step is 0.1 second.

When the time step is given, a warning is reported for each FMU with a fixed step that does not divide it.

docs.title: Communication step and internal step
docs.text:
The importer of a container (a simulation tool, or the parent of a nested container) calls it with its own communication step h; the container steps its embedded FMU's with its internal step H (its time step, times the TS_MULTIPLIER input when enabled). When h is not a multiple of H — for instance a parent at 0.01 s and a sub-container at 0.02 s — the container behaves like an FMU with a fixed internal step:

  • each internal step [T, T + H] uses the inputs of its beginning T: the values set by the importer during the step are kept for the following steps;
  • its outputs are held until the end T + H of the step;
  • the internal step is made by the call of the importer that reaches its end, and the container is at the end of every communication step.

This makes it possible to gather FMU's of different rates in sub-containers of different steps, the parent at the fastest rate (see One sub-container per sample time).

docs.title: Sequential mode
docs.text:
With the sequential option (-sequential on the command line), the Co-Simulation FMU's step one after the other in the order of the description, each one with the outputs just computed by the FMU's before it; the Model-Exchange FMU's step together after them. An FMU placed before an FMU it depends on gets the outputs of the previous step. When the order of the description does not match the order of the links between the Co-Simulation FMU's, the build reports a warning with the topological order of these FMU's:

Sequential mode: the order of the configuration does not match the topological order of the links. Topological order of the Co-Simulation FMUs: A.fmu, B.fmu, C.fmu.

Reorder the FMU's of the description to follow it. The links inside a loop (A → B → A) are not taken into account: one of them goes backwards whatever the order.

docs.title: Initialization of the embedded FMU's
docs.text:
During the initialization, the container propagates the links between its embedded FMU's, as Simulink does: each FMU is initialized with the values computed by the FMU's it depends on. When the container leaves its Initialization Mode, it takes its FMU's in the order of their links: each FMU gets its linked inputs, leaves its Initialization Mode, then its outputs are read for the FMU's after it. In a chain A → B → C, B is initialized with the outputs of A, then C with the outputs of B.

  • Loops of links (A → B → A): a loop is cut before its first FMU in the description, which is initialized with the value the link has before the propagation; the build reports a warning.
  • Outputs read during the initialization: an importer that reads an output of the container before the end of its initialization gets the value of the embedded FMU, not propagated yet: the propagation happens when the container leaves its Initialization Mode. A nested container propagates its own links.
  • Clocks and clocked variables (LS-BUS) are not propagated: they are handled once the FMU's leave the initialization.
  • The reset of an embedded FMU initializes it again with the current values of its inputs, without propagation to the other FMU's.

The FMI calls are detailed in Initialization FMI Sequence.

Several formats are supported as description files: - a CSV format: define only the routing table. Other options should be defined as command line options. - a JSON file: all parameters can be defined in the file. Command line can define default values if the parameter is not present in JSON file. - a SSP file. See ssp-standard.org. define only the routing table. Other options are defined with command line.

docs.title: Command Line Options
docs.text:
The fmucontainer command supports the following options:

Option Default Description -container filename[:step_size] (required) Description file for the container (.csv, .json, or .ssp). The optional :step_size suffix sets the internal time step (in seconds) when using .jsonor .ssp. Can be specified multiple times to build several containers. -fmu-directory path . Directory containing the source FMUs and used to generate the containers. -fmi {2\|3} 2 FMI version for the container interface. Only 2 or 3 is supported. -mt off Enable multi-threaded mode: each embedded FMU runs in its own thread. -sequential off Use sequential mode to schedule embedded FMUs. -profile off Enable profiling mode to monitor doStep() performance of each embedded FMU. -vr off Add a TS_MULTIPLIER input port to the container, allowing dynamic control of the step size. -reset-ports off Add a container.reset input to each embedded FMU, to reset it during the simulation. See Reset of Embedded FMUs. -datalog off Log input, output, and local variables of the container into a CSV file. -dump-json off Dump a JSON description file for each container. -no-auto-input auto Disable automatic exposure of unconnected input ports from embedded FMUs. -no-auto-output auto Disable automatic exposure of unconnected output ports from embedded FMUs. -no-auto-link auto Disable automatic linking of ports with matching names and types. -auto-local off Expose local variables of the embedded FMUs. -auto-parameter off Expose parameters of the embedded FMUs. -debug off Enable verbose logging during the build process, and keep the build directory (<container name>/ in the FMU directory).

Example:

fmucontainer -container assembly.csv:0.001 -fmu-directory ./my_fmus -fmi 3 -mt -profile

This command builds an FMI-3.0 container from assembly.csv with a 1 ms time step, multi-threading enabled, and profiling active. The source FMUs are located in the ./my_fmus directory.

docs.title: CSV Input file
docs.text:
This is the historic input file format. It has been superseded by the Json input file format. It cannot describe an FMU embedded several times: exporting such an assembly to CSV is refused.

Example: * Two FMU's to be assembled: bb_position.fmu and bb_velocity.fmu * Container should expose position1 from bb_position.fmu as position * Container has no input * there's two links between embedded FMU's

the container.csv file content:

rule;from_fmu;from_port;to_fmu;to_port
FMU;bb_position.fmu;;;
FMU;bb_velocity.fmu;;;
OUTPUT;bb_position.fmu;position1;;position
LINK;bb_position.fmu;is_ground;bb_velocity.fmu;reset
LINK;bb_velocity.fmu;velocity;bb_position.fmu;velocity
OUTPUT;bb_velocity.fmu;velocity;;

Asserting the FMU's and the CSV files are located in current working directory, the following command will build the container:

fmucontainer -container container.csv:0.1

Then container.fmu should be available. Note: the optional :0.1 suffix means the timestep should be 0.1 second.

docs.title: Json Input file
docs.text: fmucontainer -container container.json

docs.title: Embedding the same FMU several times
docs.text:
Each embedded FMU is designated by its name in the link, input, output, start and drop blocks. Usually, the name is the path of the FMU file. To embed the same FMU several times in one container, give each instance its own name, and its file in the optional path block:

{
  "name": "two_balls.fmu",
  "fmu": ["bb_position.fmu", "bb_velocity.fmu", "bb_position-1.fmu", "bb_velocity-1.fmu"],
  "path": {"bb_position-1.fmu": "bb_position.fmu", "bb_velocity-1.fmu": "bb_velocity.fmu"},
  "link": [["bb_position.fmu", "is_ground", "bb_velocity.fmu", "reset"],
           ["bb_velocity.fmu", "velocity", "bb_position.fmu", "velocity"],
           ["bb_position-1.fmu", "is_ground", "bb_velocity-1.fmu", "reset"],
           ["bb_velocity-1.fmu", "velocity", "bb_position-1.fmu", "velocity"]],
  "output": [["bb_position.fmu", "position1", "position"],
             ["bb_position-1.fmu", "position1", "position_2"]]
}
  • The path block maps an instance name to its FMU file; a name absent from it is its own file. It is written only when the assembly has instances, so other descriptions are unchanged.
  • The tools name the instances <stem>-<n>.fmu (bb_position-1.fmu, bb_position-2.fmu...), with the smallest free n; any name unique in its container is accepted.
  • Each instance is a distinct embedded FMU: it is extracted in its own directory of the container, its library is loaded from there, and it is instantiated under its own name (<container instance>.<instance name>).
  • fmusplit writes one FMU file per instance (bb_position.fmu, bb_position-1.fmu...), so the JSON it produces needs no path block.

docs.title: SSP Input file
docs.text:
This feature is still alpha. User interface may change in the future.

The following command 

fmucontainer -container my_file.ssp:0.1

will generate an FMU container :

  1. extract FMU's from the SSP file
  2. build a container accordingly to the SSP

Note: the optional :0.1 suffix means the timestep should be 0.1 second.

Several components of the SSP may share one FMU source: each of them is embedded as an instance of that FMU (model.fmu, then model-1.fmu...).

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: FMU Containers can also be created programmatically using the Python API. This is the most flexible approach for automation and CI/CD pipelines.

docs.title: Using a Description File
docs.text:
The Assembly class can load an existing description file (CSV, JSON, or SSP) and build the container:

from pathlib import Path
from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.assembly import Assembly

# Load a CSV description and build the container
assembly = Assembly("bouncing.json",
                    fmu_directory=Path("containers/bouncing_ball"),
                    default_mt=True)
assembly.make_fmu()

You can also export the assembly to a different format:

# Export the assembly as JSON (useful for review or version control)
# FMU paths (fmu, link, input, output, start, drop blocks) are automatically
# made relative to the directory of "bouncing.json".
assembly.write_json("bouncing.json")

# Export back to CSV
assembly.write_csv("bouncing-export.csv")

Basename-only export

Pass basenames_only=True to write_json() to reference embedded FMUs only by their filename (no directory) instead of a path relative to the JSON's location. This is useful when the JSON's own physical location has no lasting meaning (e.g. a documentation copy written to a temporary directory before being embedded inside a built FMU).

docs.title: Building a Container Programmatically
docs.text:
For full control without any description file, use the FMUContainer class directly. The following example builds a bouncing ball container from scratch:

from pathlib import Path
from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.container import FMUContainer

fmu_directory = Path("containers/bouncing_ball")

# Create the container
container = FMUContainer("bouncing", fmu_directory, fmi_version=2)

# Load the embedded FMUs
container.get_fmu("bb_position.fmu")
container.get_fmu("bb_velocity.fmu")

# Expose outputs: (from_fmu, from_port, exposed_name)
container.add_output("bb_position.fmu", "position1", "position")
container.add_output("bb_velocity.fmu", "velocity", "velocity")

# Create links between embedded FMUs
container.add_link("bb_position.fmu", "is_ground", "bb_velocity.fmu", "reset")
container.add_link("bb_velocity.fmu", "velocity", "bb_position.fmu", "velocity")

# Automatically expose remaining unconnected inputs/outputs
container.add_implicit_rule(auto_input=True, auto_output=True, auto_link=True)

# Build the FMU container
container.make_fmu("bouncing.fmu", step_size=0.1, mt=True)

The resulting bouncing.fmu is generated in the fmu_directory. The container is assembled in the directory fmu_directory/<container name without .fmu> (bouncing/ here), which is deleted after the build, unless debug=True: make sure no directory of yours has that name. make_fmu can be called several times on the same FMUContainer, e.g. to build several variants.

The methods defining the topology raise FMUContainerError when a rule cannot be applied: unknown FMU or port, wrong causality, incompatible types or dimensions, input already fed, start value of the wrong format.

docs.title: FMUContainer Reference
docs.text:
The FMUContainer constructor takes the following parameters:

Parameter Default Description identifier (required) used as modelIdentifier in modelDescription.xml fmu_directory (required) Directory containing the source FMUs fmi_version 2 FMI version for the container interface (2 or 3) reset_ports False Add a container.reset input to each embedded FMU (see Reset of Embedded FMUs)

The following methods define the container topology:

Method Description get_fmu(fmu_filename, name=None) Load an embedded FMU from fmu_directory; name designates an instance of an FMU embedded several times (e.g. get_fmu("model.fmu", "model-1.fmu")), then used by the other methods add_input(exposed_name, fmu_name, port_name) Expose a port of an embedded FMU as a container input add_output(fmu_name, port_name, exposed_name) Expose a port of an embedded FMU as a container output add_link(from_fmu, from_port, to_fmu, to_port) Connect an output to an input between embedded FMUs drop_port(fmu_name, port_name) Explicitly ignore an output port add_start_value(fmu_name, port_name, value) Set a start value for a port of an embedded FMU add_implicit_rule(auto_input, auto_output, auto_link, auto_parameter, auto_local) Automatically wire unconnected ports make_fmu(filename, step_size, mt, profiling, sequential, ts_multiplier, datalog) Build the container FMU

The make_fmu method accepts the following parameters:

Parameter Default Description fmu_filename (required) Output filename for the container step_size None Internal time step in seconds (deduced from embedded FMUs if not set) mt False Enable multi-threading sequential False Use sequential scheduling profiling False Enable profiling ts_multiplier False Add TS_MULTIPLIER input for dynamic step size control datalog False Log variables into a CSV file

docs.title: FMI Support
docs.text:
FMI-3.0 current support is limited. Feel free to create a ticket to let us know your needs.

A container may embed FMU's in Co-Simulation mode as well as in Model-Exchange mode, and both kinds can be freely mixed inside the same container. The mode used for each embedded FMU is detected automatically — see Model-Exchange support below.

docs.title: FMI-2.0 Containers
docs.text: Without any additional option, fmucontainer will produce FMI-2.0 containers. These containers may embed - FMU 2.0 in cosimulation mode without any particular limitation. - FMU 2.0 in Model-Exchange mode. - FMU 3.0 in cosimulation mode with limitations: - Variables with FMI-3.0 specific types can be used for routing but cannot be exposed (as input, output, parameter or local). Note: boolean is redefined in FMI-3.0. So cannot be exposed from an FMU-3.0. - Early Return feature is not supported - Arrays are not supported - FMU 3.0 in Model-Exchange mode (same type/exposition limitations as above).

docs.title: FMI-3.0 Containers
docs.text:
To produce FMI-3.0 compliant containers, use option -fmi 3 in fmucontainer command line. Those containers may embed

  • FMU 2.0 in cosimulation mode with limitations:

  • boolean variables can be used for routing but cannot be exposed (as input, output, parameter or local).

  • FMU 2.0 in Model-Exchange mode.

  • FMU 3.0 in cosimulation mode with limitations:

  • Early Return feature is not supported

  • Arrays are not supported

  • FMU 3.0 in Model-Exchange mode.

docs.title: Model-Exchange support
docs.text:
In addition to Co-Simulation, fmucontainer can embed Model-Exchange (ME) FMU's. In that case the container itself provides the numerical solver: it integrates the continuous states of the embedded ME FMU's and handles their events.

Automatic mode selection

The mode of each embedded FMU is detected automatically from its modelDescription.xml; there is no command-line option to select it:

  • An FMU that only provides Model-Exchange is embedded in Model-Exchange mode.
  • An FMU that provides both Co-Simulation and Model-Exchange is embedded in Co-Simulation mode (Co-Simulation takes precedence).

How it works:

  • All Model-Exchange FMU's are advanced together by a built-in fixed-step solver (forward Euler), using the container's time_step as the integration step. Keep the step small enough for the dynamics of your ME models.
  • State events (via event indicators) and time events are detected and handled so that the coupled set of ME FMU's stays consistent.
  • During the integration, only the couplings between ME FMU's are exchanged at each evaluation of the solver: the inputs fed by Co-Simulation FMU's or by the importer do not change during a step, they are set once per step.
  • The number of continuous states (nx) and of event indicators (nz) is computed automatically from the FMU's <ModelStructure> (FMI-2.0 <Derivatives> / FMI-3.0 <ContinuousStateDerivative> and <EventIndicator>). You can inspect these values with fmudump, which now reports nx and nz for any FMU providing Model-Exchange.
  • Both FMI-2.0 and FMI-3.0 Model-Exchange FMU's are supported, in either an FMI-2.0 or an FMI-3.0 container. The routing/exposition rules and type limitations listed above apply identically to Model-Exchange FMU's.

No change to the description file (CSV/JSON/SSP) nor to the Python API is required: simply reference a Model-Exchange FMU like any other embedded FMU and build the container as usual.

docs.title: Connecting FMI-2 and FMI-3 arrays
docs.text:
FMI-2 has no native array concept: vectors and matrices are conventionally exposed as a set of scalar ports using the Modelica-style notation name[i,j,...]. FMI-3 defines arrays as first-class variables carrying one or more <Dimension> elements.

fmucontainer bridges the two, for 1D and multi-dimensional arrays:

  • When an embedded FMI-2 FMU exposes a set of ports sharing a common basename and covering a full N-dimensional hyperrectangle (e.g. M[1,1], M[1,2], M[2,1], M[2,2]), a virtual aggregated port named basename is automatically created with dimensions matching the detected shape.
  • Elements are flattened in row-major order (last index varies fastest), matching the FMI-3 array memory layout, so the aggregate can be linked directly to an FMI-3 array port of matching type and shape, in either direction (FMI-2 → FMI-3 or FMI-3 → FMI-2).
  • The individual scalar ports remain available and can still be used element-by-element if desired.
  • When the aggregate is linked, each underlying scalar element port is also marked as connected (rule LINK), so it will not be picked up by auto_input / auto_output.

Example — 1D vector. Connect a 3-element vector produced by an FMI-2 FMU to a 3-dimensional array consumed by an FMI-3 FMU:

rule;from_fmu;from_port;to_fmu;to_port
FMU;fmi2_producer.fmu;;;
FMU;fmi3_consumer.fmu;;;
LINK;fmi2_producer.fmu;myVector;fmi3_consumer.fmu;myArray

The scalar ports myVector[1], myVector[2], myVector[3] of fmi2_producer.fmu are transparently mapped onto the single myArray array port (dimension 3) of fmi3_consumer.fmu.

Example — 2D matrix. Connect a 2×3 matrix exposed as 6 scalar ports in FMI-2 to a 2×3 FMI-3 array:

rule;from_fmu;from_port;to_fmu;to_port
FMU;fmi2_producer.fmu;;;
FMU;fmi3_consumer.fmu;;;
LINK;fmi2_producer.fmu;M;fmi3_consumer.fmu;M

with fmi2_producer.fmu declaring M[1,1], M[1,2], M[1,3], M[2,1], M[2,2], M[2,3], and fmi3_consumer.fmu declaring M with <Dimension start="2"/><Dimension start="3"/>.

Element-by-element linking remains fully supported:

LINK;fmi2_producer.fmu;M[1,1];fmi3_consumer.fmu;M[1,1]
LINK;fmi2_producer.fmu;M[1,2];fmi3_consumer.fmu;M[1,2]
...

Notes and limitations:

  • The aggregate is only created when indices form a complete, contiguous N-dimensional hyperrectangle starting at 0 or 1 on every axis. Missing elements, duplicates, or heterogeneous ranks abort the aggregation (scalar elements remain usable individually).
  • All aggregated elements must share the same type, causality, variability and clock.
  • If a scalar port with the same name as the would-be aggregate already exists, the aggregate is not created (no ambiguity).
  • Elements are always flattened in row-major order to match FMI-3. If the FMI-2 FMU documents its 2D array in column-major, transpose the FMI-3 side accordingly.
  • Aggregated FMI-2 array ports can only be linked between embedded FMUs — they cannot be exposed as container inputs/outputs in an FMI-2 container (an FMI-2 container has no way to expose a native array).

docs.title: Multi-Threading
docs.text:
If enabled through MT flag, each FMU will be run using its own thread which 1. fetch its inputs from container buffer which is shared with all FMUs. 2. process DoStep()

Synchronization uses a mutex.

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text: If enabled through profiling flag, each call to DoStep of each FMU is monitored. The elapsed time is compared with currentCommunicationPoint and a RT ratio is computed. A ratio greater than 1.0 means this particular FMU is faster than RT.

docs.title: Container with datalog
docs.text:
To facilitate debugging of FMUs assemblies, the datalog feature is extremely helpful.

You can enable datalog in two ways:

  • CLI: add the -datalog option to the fmucontainer command.
  • GUI: in FMU Container Builder, open Configuration and check Enable Datalog before saving.

When enabled, a CSV file is automatically generated. The file name is derived from the FMU container’s name and contains the values of all signals exchanged during the simulation, recorded at each container time step.

docs.title: CSV format
docs.text:
• The first line holds the names of the columns: time, then one column per signal.
  • Each following line is one container time step. Real values are written with every significant digit (17 for a Float64, 9 for a Float32) and always with a decimal dot, whatever the locale of the simulation tool: the time and the values read back from the file are exactly those of the simulation.
  • A string, or a column name, that contains a comma, a double quote or a line break is enclosed in double quotes, its double quotes being doubled (RFC 4180): "a[1,2]", "say ""hi""". Spreadsheets and the Python csv module read it as one field.
  • Binaries are written in hexadecimal, booleans and clocks as 0 or 1.

docs.title: FMU Container Builder — GUI
docs.text: The FMU Container Builder provides a visual, node-graph interface to assemble multiple FMUs into a single FMU Container — without writing JSON or CSV files manually.

docs.title: Launching the Interface
docs.text:
fmucontainer-gui

Or from the FMU Toolbox Launcher, click FMU Container Build.

docs.title: Interface Overview
docs.text:
The interface is split into three main areas:

Area Description Node Graph (left) Visual canvas where FMU nodes and wires are displayed Tree View (top-right) Hierarchical structure of containers and FMUs Detail Panel (bottom-right) Properties of the selected node, wire, or container Button Bar (bottom) Configuration, load/save, and export actions Status Bar (very bottom) Last log message; click it to open the log window

docs.title: Node Graph
docs.text: The node graph is the central workspace where you visually compose your FMU container.

docs.title: Adding FMU Nodes
docs.text:
There are three ways to add FMUs to the canvas:

  • Drag & Drop: drag .fmu files from your file manager directly onto the canvas.
  • Right-click → Add FMU…: opens a file dialog to select one or more .fmu files.
  • Tree View → Right-click → Add FMU…: adds FMUs under a specific container in the hierarchy.

Each FMU node displays its name as a title: the filename of its FMU. The same FMU can be added several times: each new node is an instance of it, named <stem>-<n>.fmu with the smallest free n (bb_position-1.fmu, bb_position-2.fmu...); another file with an already used filename is named the same way. The FMU detail panel of an instance shows the FMU it is an instance of. Wires, start values and exposed ports belong to one node, and a saved JSON keeps the file of each instance (see Embedding the same FMU several times).

Instances and automatic rules

The instances of an FMU are never linked by auto_link: wire them explicitly. When auto_input or auto_output exposes a port whose name is already used, it is exposed as <fmu>.<port> (e.g. bb_position-1.position1).

Title bar color — Co-Simulation vs Model-Exchange

The color of a node's title bar reflects the FMI interface used to embed the FMU:

  • Blue — the FMU is embedded in Co-Simulation mode (default). FMUs advertising both Co-Simulation and Model-Exchange are also shown in blue, since Co-Simulation takes precedence.
  • Green — the FMU only provides Model-Exchange and is therefore integrated by the container's built-in solver (see Model-Exchange support).

This lets you tell at a glance which embedded FMUs rely on the container's solver.

docs.title: Connecting FMUs with Wires
docs.text:
To create a connection between two FMUs:

  1. Click and drag from the body of a node (below its title bar)
  2. Release on another node
  3. A wire is created between the two nodes

Title bar vs body

  • Title bar (top strip with the FMU name): click to select or drag to move the node.
  • Body (area below the title bar): drag to create a wire.

The cursor changes on hover to indicate the available action: ✥ for move, ✛ for wire creation.

Wires are directional — arrowheads indicate the data-flow direction:

  • Arrow on one end → data flows in that direction (from one FMU to the other)
  • Arrows on both ends → bidirectional connection (each FMU feeds the other)

The direction is determined by the port mappings configured in the Wire Details panel.

docs.title: Reshaping Wires with Waypoints
docs.text:
Wires are drawn as straight-line segments. You can add waypoints to create broken lines and route wires around nodes for better readability.

Action How Add a waypoint Double-click on a wire Move a waypoint Drag the blue handle (visible when the wire is selected) Remove a waypoint Double-click on a blue handle

You can add as many waypoints as needed. The wire becomes a polyline passing through each waypoint in order.

Visibility

Waypoint handles are only visible when the wire is selected. Click on a wire to select it and reveal its handles.

docs.title: Navigating the Canvas
docs.text: Action How Pan Middle-click drag, or Alt+Left Button drag Zoom Mouse wheel Fit all Right-click → Fit View Select Left-click on a node or wire Multi-select Rubber-band selection (left-click drag on empty space) Move node Left-click drag on a node Delete Select items, then press Del or Backspace

docs.title: Context Menu (Right-click on Canvas)
docs.text: Action Description Add FMU… Open file dialog to add FMU nodes Delete Selection Remove selected nodes and wires Info Show node information and optionally replace the FMU file (single node only) Open in FMU Editor Open the selected FMU in the Variable Editor (single node only) Open in FMU Tool Open the selected FMU in FMU Tool (single node only) Fit View Zoom to fit all nodes in the viewport

docs.title: Replacing an FMU
docs.text:
To replace an FMU with a different version or an alternative file:

  1. Select the node, right-click and choose Info
  2. The dialog shows the node name and current FMU file path
  3. Click Browse… to select a new .fmu file
  4. Click OK to apply the replacement

The replacement is done in place, for the selected node only, even when it is an instance of an FMU added several times: all wires, start values, and exposed input/output ports are preserved. The node is renamed after the new file (with the smallest free -<n> suffix if that name is used). If a port name referenced by a start value, a wire mapping, or an exposed input/output no longer exists in the new FMU, it appears in red in the detail panels — allowing you to review and correct invalid references. The affected wire itself is also drawn in red on the canvas, so broken connections are immediately visible without having to open every wire's details.

Typical use case

Use this feature when a new version of an FMU is available: replace the file and instantly see which connections or start values need updating.

docs.title: Tree View
docs.text: The tree view shows the hierarchical structure of your container assembly.

docs.title: Root Container
docs.text: The top-level item represents the output container FMU (default name: container.fmu). All FMU nodes and sub-containers are children of this root.

docs.title: Sub-Containers
docs.text:
You can create nested containers to organize complex assemblies:

  • Right-click → Add Container: creates a new sub-container under the selected item.
  • Rename: right-click on a container → Rename.
  • Drag & Drop: reorganize nodes and sub-containers by dragging them within the tree.

After renaming a container, the Container Details panel is refreshed immediately to reflect the new name.

docs.title: Step Size Column
docs.text:
The second column of the tree view shows the step size of each item, in seconds. It is informative: it cannot be edited.

  • FMU: the step size declared by the FMU (stepSize of its DefaultExperiment); empty if the FMU declares none.
  • Container: its step_size parameter (see Container Details). When step_size is empty, the column shows, in italics, the step size deduced when the container is built: the least common multiple of the step sizes of the FMUs that cannot handle a variable step size or, if all of them can, the largest step size; 0.1 s if no FMU declares a step size. A sub-container counts as an FMU that can handle a variable step size.

The column is updated when FMUs or containers are added, moved, replaced or removed, and when step_size is changed.

docs.title: Context Menu (Right-click on Tree View)
docs.text: Action Description Add FMU… Add FMU nodes under the selected container Add Container Create a new sub-container Rename Rename a container Delete Remove a node or container (and all its contents)

docs.title: Detail Panel
docs.text: The detail panel shows the properties of the currently selected element.

docs.title: Node (FMU) Details
docs.text:
When an FMU node is selected, the detail panel shows:

  • FMU name, generator tool, and step size
  • Three tabs: Start Values, Input Ports, and Output Ports

docs.title: Start Values tab
docs.text:
Lists all input and parameter ports with their start values.

Column Description Input Port Port name (read-only). Clock and binary ports, as well as FMI-2 array aggregates, are excluded. Start Value User-defined start value (editable). A gray placeholder shows the FMU's default value.

Start Values

Leave the start value empty to use the FMU's built-in default. Enter a value to override it in the container.

FMI-2 array aggregates

Virtual array aggregates (see Port Style Indicators) are not listed in this tab. Start values must be defined on the individual scalar elements (myVector[1], myVector[2], …), which appear as regular input ports.

docs.title: Input Ports tab
docs.text:
Lists all input ports with a checkbox to explicitly expose them at the container level.

Column Description Input Port Port name (read-only) Exposed Checkbox — when checked, the port is exposed as an input of the container

When to expose inputs

By default, auto_input automatically exposes unconnected input ports. Use this tab to explicitly select which inputs to expose — useful when auto_input is disabled, when the port is also driven by a wire but should remain overridable from outside the container, or when you need fine-grained control and want the assembly description to declare the input explicitly rather than relying on auto-wiring.

Nested containers

When an FMU with an exposed input is nested inside a sub-container, the input is automatically propagated up through each parent container so that it remains reachable from the root container.

docs.title: Output Ports tab
docs.text:
Lists all output ports with a checkbox to explicitly expose them at the container level.

Column Description Output Port Port name (read-only) Exposed Checkbox — when checked, the port is exposed as an output of the container

When to expose outputs

By default, auto_output automatically exposes unconnected output ports. Use this tab to explicitly select which outputs to expose — useful when auto_output is disabled or when you need fine-grained control.

Nested containers

When an FMU with an exposed output is nested inside a sub-container, the output is automatically propagated up through each parent container so that it remains reachable from the root container.

Port Style Indicators

Ports are displayed with different text styles to indicate their nature:

  • Parameter ports are shown in italics — these are configuration values or tuning parameters.
  • FMI-2 array aggregates are shown in bold — these are virtual ports representing a family of scalar variables named basename[k] or basename[i,j,...] (Modelica-style comma notation) that the toolbox groups together so they can be connected as a single array to an FMI-3 array port.
  • When an aggregate is also a parameter, it is displayed in bold italics.
  • Other port types (standard inputs/outputs) appear in regular text.

This visual distinction helps you quickly identify parameters and array aggregates in the interface.

docs.title: Wire Details
docs.text:
When a wire is selected, the detail panel shows the variable-level mappings between the two connected FMUs.

A header label identifies the two nodes: A = first FMU, B = second FMU.

The mappings are split into three tabs:

Tab Description A → B Output ports of A connected to input ports of B B → A Output ports of B connected to input ports of A Terminals Terminal-to-terminal connections (e.g. for LS-BUS enabled FMUs)

Each tab contains a 2-column table:

Column Description Output Port Output variable of the source FMU (combo-box) Input Port Input variable of the destination FMU (combo-box)

Port Style Indicators

Ports are displayed with different text styles to indicate their nature:

  • Parameter ports are shown in italics — these are typically tuning parameters or configuration values.
  • FMI-2 array aggregates are shown in bold — virtual ports that group a family of scalar variables (e.g. myVector[1], myVector[2], myVector[3]) into a single array port. Selecting an aggregate on one side of a wire connects all its elements at once, which is especially useful for wiring FMI-2 arrays to FMI-3 array ports of matching shape.
  • When an aggregate is also a parameter, it is displayed in bold italics.
  • Other ports (standard inputs, outputs) appear in regular text.

This visual distinction helps you quickly identify parameters and array aggregates when configuring mappings.

Each tab has its own Add link / Remove link buttons to manage mappings for that direction.

Invalid connections shown in red

A wire is drawn in red on the canvas whenever at least one of its port mappings is invalid: either because the referenced port no longer exists on the FMU (e.g. after Replace FMU), or because it targets an inactive configuration node port (ts_multiplier unchecked). In both cases, the invalid port name is also shown in red inside the Wire Details table so you can quickly locate and fix (or simply understand) the broken mapping.

Direction indicator on the wire

While the Wire Details panel is open, a yellow indicator is overlaid on the selected wire to reflect the currently active tab:

  • A → B — an enlarged yellow arrowhead at the B extremity, pointing outward.
  • B → A — an enlarged yellow arrowhead at the A extremity, pointing outward.
  • Terminals — a divergent ◀▶ marker (two triangles pointing outward) at the middle of the wire.

Switching tabs updates the indicator immediately, making it easy to see which side of the connection you are currently editing.

docs.title: Terminals tab
docs.text:
The Terminals tab allows connecting FMU terminals (as defined in the FMI LS-BUS standard). Each row maps a terminal from FMU A to a terminal from FMU B:

Column Description Terminal A Terminal name from FMU A (combo-box) Terminal B Terminal name from FMU B (combo-box)

This tab is useful when working with LS-BUS enabled FMUs where communication occurs through terminal connections rather than individual variable ports.

The arrowheads on the wire update automatically to reflect the configured directions.

Below the tabs, global buttons are available:

Button Description Link Assistant Open the Link Assistant to define many links at once Remove All Remove all link definitions between A and B (both directions) Import Import link definitions from a CSV file Export Export link definitions to a CSV file

CSV Format for Import/Export

The CSV file uses 4 columns: FMU From, Port From, FMU To, Port To. Each row represents a single port-to-port connection, and both directions (A → B and B → A) are included in the same file. This makes it easy to edit link definitions in a spreadsheet and re-import them.

docs.title: Link Assistant
docs.text:
When the FMUs have hundreds of ports, filling the tables of the Wire Details panel one link at a time is tedious. The Link Assistant button opens a window that proposes links in bulk, lets you review them, and writes them into the wire only when you click Apply.

The window works on the wire that was selected when it was opened. It does not block the rest of the Container Builder: you can keep looking at the graph. Clicking Link Assistant again brings it to the front; on another wire, it closes the open assistant first (asking for confirmation if links are staged there).

Header — the two FMUs in the order of the current direction (source.fmu → target.fmu). Below each name, the counters of its ports:

Symbol Meaning Σ Total number of outputs (source) or inputs (target) ● Outputs already linked on this wire, or inputs already fed: by a link of any wire of the FMU, by an exposed input, or by a staged link ○ Free ports

The selector on the right switches the direction (A → B / B → A). The staged links of both directions are kept, so both directions can be prepared before applying.

The window has two tabs, Rules and Manual, which share the list of staged links at the bottom.

docs.title: Rules tab
docs.text:
A criterion proposes, for each free output, the input it should be linked to. Choose it with Match by:

Criterion Parameters Example Same name — vehicle.speed → vehicle.speed Replace prefix / suffix Prefix and suffix of the output name, replaced by those of the input name engine.out.speed → ecu.in.engine_speed (engine.out. → ecu.in.engine_) Regular expression A regular expression matching the whole output name, and the input name built from its groups (\1, \2, …) sensor\.(\w+)\.(\w+) → sensor_\2_\1 Similar names Minimum similarity score (1.00 to 0.50) chassis.pressure → chassis.press

Options of the criterion:

Option Effect ignore case and separators Names are compared without case nor separators (. _ - [ ] and spaces), for every criterion: Throttle_Pos matches throttle.pos. Checked by default parameters as targets Also propose the parameters of the target FMU, not only its inputs Allow only: compatible types Checked (default): a link between types without conversion is an error ✖. Unchecked: it is only a warning ⚠ Allow only: same units Checked: a link between different units is an error ✖. Unchecked (default): it is a warning ⚠

docs.title: How a criterion finds the input
docs.text:
Every criterion works the same way: it takes the free outputs one by one, in the order of the source FMU, builds from the name of each one the name of an input, and looks for that name among the free inputs of the target FMU. An output whose name does not fit the criterion, or whose input does not exist, gets no suggestion.

  • With ignore case and separators, the name built is compared to the input names without case nor separators: ecu.in.engine_speed finds the input ECU_In_Engine_Speed.
  • An input is proposed only once: when two outputs lead to the same input (engine.out.speed and engine.out.Speed), only the first one gets a suggestion.
  • Same name builds the name of the output itself; Similar names does not build a name, it looks for the closest input name (see the score below).

docs.title: Replace prefix / suffix
docs.text:
The four fields read as a rewriting of the name: Output: prefix … suffix → Input: prefix … suffix. The … stands for the rest of the name, kept as is.

  1. The output name must start with the output prefix and end with the output suffix; the other outputs are skipped.
  2. The prefix and the suffix are removed: what remains is the core of the name. It cannot be empty: an output named exactly engine.out. is skipped.
  3. The input name is the input prefix, followed by the core, followed by the input suffix.

With the output prefix engine.out. and the input prefix ecu.in.engine_ (suffixes empty), as in the screenshot at the top of the Link Assistant section:

Output Core Input looked for engine.out.speed speed ecu.in.engine_speed engine.out.torque_max torque_max ecu.in.engine_torque_max engine.in.speed — none: the output does not start with engine.out.

Other uses:

Output prefix Output suffix Input prefix Input suffix Example (empty) _meas (empty) _cmd throttle_meas → throttle_cmd bus1. _out ecu. _in bus1.speed_out → ecu.speed_in

Things to know

  • An empty field means no prefix (or no suffix), not anything. To replace only a suffix, leave both prefixes empty; with the four fields empty, the criterion is Same name.
  • The fields are plain text: no wildcard, and . is a dot. When the part to replace is not at the start or at the end of the name (e.g. engine.<anything>.out.speed), use a regular expression.
  • With ignore case and separators, the fields too are compared without case nor separators: engine.out. also takes Engine_Out_Torque, and typing engine_out_ gives the same result. Unchecked, everything is compared character by character.

docs.title: Regular expression
docs.text:
Two fields: the pattern, applied to the output name, and the replacement, which builds the input name. They use the syntax of Python regular expressions (re module).

  1. The pattern must match the whole output name, as if it began with ^ and ended with $ (writing them is allowed). The outputs it does not match are skipped.
  2. The parts of the pattern in parentheses are the groups, numbered from left to right. The replacement uses them with \1, \2, …
  3. The name built by the replacement is looked for among the free inputs.

With the pattern sensor\.(\w+)\.(\w+) and the replacement sensor_\2_\1:

Output \1 \2 Input looked for sensor.front.temp front temp sensor_temp_front sensor.rear.pressure rear pressure sensor_pressure_rear sensor.front.temp.raw — — none: \w+ does not take the . of .raw, so the pattern does not match the whole name

Useful syntax in the pattern:

Pattern Matches \. A dot. A plain . matches any character .* / .+ Any text, possibly empty / of at least one character \w+ A word: letters, digits and _, but not . nor [ \d+ A number (…) A group, reused in the replacement (?:…) Parentheses that are not a group, e.g. (?:out|output) for out or output [._] One character among . and _ \[(\d+)\] An array index such as [3]: the brackets must be escaped

In the replacement:

Replacement Gives \1, \2, … The text of the group 1, 2, … \g<0> The whole output name \g<1>0 The group 1 followed by the digit 0 (\10 would be the group 10) \g<pos> The group named pos in the pattern: (?P<pos>\w+)

More examples:

Pattern Replacement Example engine\.out\.(.*) ecu.in.engine_\1 engine.out.speed → ecu.in.engine_speed pump\[(\d+)\]\.speed pump\1_speed pump[2].speed → pump2_speed (.*)\.(?:out|output) \1.in valve.out → valve.in, pump.output → pump.in

Things to know

  • A group is written \1 in the replacement; $1, used by other tools, is taken literally.
  • ignore case and separators makes the pattern ignore the case, not the separators: the pattern applies to the real output name, so write its separators as they are (engine\.out), or accept several (engine[._]out). The name built by the replacement is then compared to the inputs without case nor separators: ecu.in.engine_\1 also finds ecu_in_Engine_Speed.
  • A pattern that is not a valid regular expression is framed in red, and gives no suggestion.

docs.title: Similar names
docs.text:
The score compares the output name to each input name (both without case nor separators when the option is checked): 1.00 for identical names, lower as they differ. For each output, the input with the best score above the threshold is proposed. A suggestion whose score is below 1.00 gets a ⚠ status, to be reviewed, unless it is already ✖.

The suggestions are updated a moment after each change of the criterion, of its parameters or of an option. Each one is checked when it can be applied, and gets a status:

Status Meaning ✔ The link can be applied ⚠ The link can be applied, but should be reviewed: lossy type conversion (e.g. Real → Int32), different units, or a name found by Similar names ✖ The link cannot be applied: the input is already fed, the types cannot be converted, the arrays have different sizes

Review the suggestions (the Show selector and the Filter field narrow the table), then click Stage checked links ↓; a double-click on a row stages that suggestion only. Check all and Uncheck all act on the rows shown. The staged links leave the suggestions; the other suggestions keep their check boxes. Then pick another criterion: it only sees the ports still free.

Typical sequence

Start with Same name, stage; then Replace prefix / suffix or Regular expression for the families of signals named differently, stage; then Similar names for what is left, reviewing each suggestion; link the last ports in the Manual tab.

Large FMUs

If a search takes more than 0.3 s (e.g. Similar names on FMUs with thousands of ports), the suggestions are no longer updated while typing: a Run ▶ button appears to search again.

docs.title: Manual tab
docs.text:
The outputs of the source FMU (left) and the inputs of the target FMU (right), each list below the name of its FMU, with the type, unit and description of each port. Narrow them with the Filter field (name or description) and the type selector; only free ports hides the ports already linked, fed or staged; show parameters also lists the parameters of the target FMU.

Select ports in both lists (Shift / Ctrl for several), check the preview below Link selection ↓, and click it:

  • as many outputs as inputs: they are paired in the order of the lists;
  • one output and several inputs: the output feeds every selected input.

docs.title: Staged links
docs.text:
The links staged by both tabs, with their direction, their origin (criterion or manual) and their status. The status is computed again on each change: two staged links feeding the same input are both ✖.

Button Description Remove selected / Remove All Remove staged links; their ports are free again and the suggestions of the Rules tab come back Cancel Close the window without changing the wire (asks for confirmation if links are staged) Apply n links Add the staged links to the wire, then close the window. Disabled while a link is ✖

The links already defined on the wire are kept. If an input was fed in the Wire Details panel while the assistant was open, its staged link is not added (a message tells how many).

FMI-2 arrays

An FMI-2 array aggregate and its elements (e.g. u and u[1], u[2]) are one input for the assistant: staging one of them takes the others, and an aggregate is linked only to an array of the same size.

Settings kept for the session

The parameters of each criterion and ignore case and separators are kept until the Container Builder is closed. The assistant always opens on Same name.

docs.title: Container Details
docs.text:
When a container is selected in the tree view, the detail panel shows its configuration parameters:

Parameter Type Description step_size text Fixed time step (in seconds) for the container's internal solver; when empty, deduced from the embedded FMUs (see Step Size Column) mt checkbox Enable multi-threading (each FMU runs in its own thread) profiling checkbox Enable performance profiling of embedded FMUs sequential checkbox Force sequential execution order auto_link checkbox Automatically link ports with matching names and types auto_input checkbox Automatically expose unconnected input ports auto_output checkbox Automatically expose unconnected output ports auto_parameter checkbox Automatically expose parameter ports auto_local checkbox Automatically expose local variables ts_multiplier checkbox Add a TS_MULTIPLIER input for dynamic step size control reset_ports checkbox Add a reset input to each FMU of the container (see Reset of Embedded FMUs)

docs.title: The configuration Node
docs.text:
As soon as at least one sub-container (not the root container) has its ts_multiplier parameter checked, or one container (the root included) has its reset_ports parameter checked, a virtual node titled configuration automatically appears on the canvas. This node is a visual aid: it does not correspond to any real FMU file, and it never gets its own row in the tree view — it exists purely to help you keep track of which FMU drives the TS_MULTIPLIER input of which sub-container, and the reset of which FMU.

  • The node exposes one input port per checked sub-container, named <container_name>.ts_multiplier (the .fmu suffix of the container name is stripped).
  • It also exposes one Boolean input port per FMU, or sub-container, of each container with reset_ports checked, named <fmu_name>.reset (the .fmu suffix is stripped): see Reset of Embedded FMUs.
  • It can be wired from any FMU in the assembly, like a regular node — drag from the FMU's body onto the configuration node body to create the wire.
  • It can be moved freely but cannot be deleted manually while it is still relevant.
  • Selecting the configuration node shows its reset ports, each with an Exposed checkbox: an exposed port becomes the input container.<fmu>.reset of the container of the FMU (the ports are exposed anyway when auto_input is checked).
  • Checking ts_multiplier on the root container has no effect: the root container is never added to the configuration node. reset_ports applies to the root container too.

This wire is a real link, not just a visual note

Unlike the configuration node itself (a pure GUI convenience), a wire connected to it is exported: it corresponds to a real link driving the target sub-container's reserved container.ts_multiplier runtime input (the actual input FMI port exposed by that container when ts_multiplier is enabled), or the reserved container.reset input of the FMU. When importing a JSON or FMU container, a link whose destination is a sub-container name with port container.ts_multiplier, or an FMU with port container.reset, is automatically reconstructed as a wire to the configuration node's matching dynamic port; an input rule on container.reset checks its Exposed box. On export, the reverse translation is applied, so the round-trip is lossless.

Unchecking ts_multiplier or reset_ports

Unchecking ts_multiplier on a sub-container (or reset_ports on a container, or moving an FMU out of it) does not delete its port nor an existing wire connected to it. Instead, the port becomes inactive and any wire referencing it is drawn in red (both on the canvas and in the Wire Details panel, see Wire Details), to flag the now-invalid connection. Re-checking ts_multiplier automatically restores the wire to a valid (non-red) state — no need to rewire.

Automatic cleanup

The configuration node is only removed from the canvas once all its ports are inactive and no wire (valid or invalid) references it anymore. This avoids losing your wiring setup when temporarily unchecking ts_multiplier on a container.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Click Configuration to open a popup menu with:

  • Generate FMI-2 / FMI-3: choose the target FMI version for the output container.
  • Verbose Mode: enable detailed logging for this window (DEBUG messages in the log window, and a copy of its log messages on the standard output of the terminal that launched the GUI) and keep intermediate build artifacts. The other windows are not affected.
  • Enable Datalog: include a datalog.txt configuration in the generated FMU (useful for simulation trace export).
  • AI Assistant On / Off: start or stop the MCP server of the AI Assistant (only when the mcp extra is installed).

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Button Description Load FMU Container Load an existing FMU container (splits it and reconstructs the graph) Import Import an assembly from a JSON or CSV description file Export as JSON Export the assembly as a JSON description file Save as FMU Container Build and save the container as a .fmu file Exit Close the window (prompts if there are unsaved changes)

During Load, Import, Export, and Save operations, a progress dialog shows execution logs in real time. These messages also remain available in the log window.

Relative FMU paths

When exporting with Export as JSON, the FMU paths written in the fmu and link blocks are automatically made relative to the directory where the JSON file is saved. This keeps the exported assembly portable as long as the FMU files stay in the same relative layout — see also the FMU location requirement when re-importing.

docs.title: Log
docs.text: Every component of the Container Builder (graph, tree, build, import, AI Assistant) writes to the log of its window. With several windows opened from the launcher, each window has its own log: an action, or a request of the AI Assistant of a window, is only logged in that window. The few messages that do not come from a window are shown in all of them.

docs.title: Status Bar
docs.text:
The status bar, under the button bar, shows the last message of level Info or above, in the colour of its level (grey for information, yellow for warnings, red for errors). It stays until the next message. A message spanning several lines is shown by its first line followed by ….

Click the status bar to open the log window.

docs.title: Log Window
docs.text:
The log window lists every message of this window since it was opened (the last 5000 ones). It is not modal: it can stay open next to the main window and receives new messages as they arrive.

Control Description Level (Debug / Info / Warning / Error) Show only the messages of this level or above Search… Show only the messages containing this text (case-insensitive) Save Logs… Save the displayed messages in a text file Clear Forget the messages of this window (they are not shown again when the log window is reopened); the other windows keep theirs Close Close the window; the log keeps being recorded

Debug messages

DEBUG messages are only recorded while Verbose Mode of the window is enabled (see Configuration).

docs.title: Step 1: Add FMUs
docs.text: Drag and drop your .fmu files onto the canvas, or use the right-click menu.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect FMUs
docs.text: Draw wires between output and input ports. Select a wire to configure the port-level mappings in the detail panel. Use Auto-connect to speed up the process.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure the Container
docs.text: Select the root container in the tree view to set the time step and other options (multi-threading, profiling, auto-linking, etc.).

docs.title: Step 4: Organize Hierarchy (Optional)
docs.text: Create sub-containers and drag FMUs into them to build nested assemblies.

docs.title: Step 5: Set Start Values and Expose Ports (Optional)
docs.text: Select individual FMU nodes and override input port start values as needed. Use the Input Ports tab to explicitly expose specific input ports, and the Output Ports tab to explicitly expose specific output ports, at the container level.

docs.title: Step 6: Save
docs.text: Click Save as FMU Container to build the final .fmu file, or Export as JSON to save the assembly description for later use with the fmucontainer CLI.

docs.title: Auto-Wiring Workflow
docs.text: If your FMUs share matching port names (e.g. the outputs of one FMU have the same names as the inputs of another), you can let the container build the connections automatically using the auto_link feature — without manually creating wires.

docs.title: Step 1: Import your FMUs
docs.text: Drag and drop your .fmu files onto the canvas, or use the right-click menu to add them. There is no need to draw wires manually between the FMUs.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable auto_link
docs.text:
Select the container in the tree view (the root item or a sub-container). In the Container Details panel, make sure the auto_link checkbox is checked (it is enabled by default).

This tells the container to automatically connect ports with matching names when the FMU is built.

docs.title: Step 3: Save the FMU Container
docs.text: Click Save as FMU Container to build the .fmu file. The auto-linking is performed during the build process: matching output and input ports are connected automatically.

docs.title: Step 4: Reload to verify
docs.text:
Click Load FMU Container and open the .fmu file you just created. The tool will split the container and reconstruct the graph — this time with all the automatically created wires visible on the canvas. You can select any wire to inspect the port mappings in the detail panel.

Combining manual and automatic wiring

Auto-linking and manual wires can coexist. Any explicit wire you create takes priority. The auto_link option will only fill in the remaining unconnected matching ports.

docs.title: Loading an Existing Container
docs.text:
Click Load FMU Container to open an existing .fmu container. The tool will:

  1. Split the container to extract the embedded FMUs and the JSON description
  2. Reconstruct the node graph with all FMUs, wires, port mappings, and start values
  3. Restore container parameters (step size, multi-threading, etc.)

You can then modify the assembly and re-save it.

docs.title: Importing an Assembly File
docs.text:
Click Import to load an assembly from an existing description file. Two formats are supported:

  • JSON — full assembly description including container parameters, FMU list, links, start values, and sub-containers.
  • CSV — routing table only (FMU list, links, inputs/outputs). Container parameters use defaults.

The tool will:

  1. Parse the description file using the same engine as the fmucontainer CLI
  2. Reconstruct the node graph with all FMUs, wires, port mappings, and start values
  3. Restore container parameters (from JSON) or apply defaults (from CSV)

FMU location

The .fmu files referenced in the description must be located in the same directory as the JSON or CSV file.

Unsaved Changes

If you have unsaved changes when closing the window or loading a new container, you will be prompted to confirm.

docs.title: Step-by-step example
docs.text:
The topology supported by fmucontainer requires a BUS Simulation FMU. (See 3.2.2 of LS-BUS specification).

  1. From LS-BUS Examples build 2 nodes node1.fmu and node2.fmu) and the Bus Simulation bus.fmu.

  2. Create a bus+nodes.json file describing the container. In this example, it connects node1.fmu to bus.fmu through their terminals and the same for node2.fmu. 

        {
      "name": "bus+nodes.fmu",
      "fmu": [
        "bus.fmu",
        "node1.fmu",
        "node2.fmu"
      ],
      "link": [
        [ "node1.fmu", "CanChannel", "bus.fmu", "Node1"],
        [ "node2.fmu", "CanChannel", "bus.fmu", "Node2"]
      ],
      "step_size": 0.1
    }

  3. Create the container with the following command line 

    fmucontainer -container bus+nodes.json -fmi 3

  4. You could run the bus+nodes.fmu with your favourite FMI-importer. Here is an example: 

    from fmpy.simulation import simulate_fmu

def log(*args):
    msg = args[-1]
    if isinstance(args[-1], bytes):
        msg = msg.decode('utf-8')
    print(f"{msg}")


simulate_fmu("bus+nodes.fmu", step_size=0.1, stop_time=1,
             output_interval=0.1, validate=True, use_event_mode=True,
             logger=log, debug_logging=True, relative_tolerance=1e-6)

docs.title: Round-trip with fmusplit
docs.text: Running fmusplit on the container bus+nodes.fmu produced above regenerates exactly the same JSON assembly, with terminal-level link entries (e.g. [ "node1.fmu", "CanChannel", "bus.fmu", "Node1" ]) rather than the underlying per-signal port links. The extracted assembly can therefore be re-imported into the GUI or rebuilt with fmucontainer without further editing.

docs.title: FMU Checker
docs.text:
FMU Manipulation Toolbox includes two built-in checkers (FMI 2.0 and 3.0). You can also write your own custom checkers.

  • OperationGenericCheck validates modelDescription.xml against the official FMI XSD schema and reports every violation.
  • OperationSemanticCheck checks the rules of the standard that the schema cannot express (FMI 2.0.5 §2.2.7–2.2.8, FMI 3.0.2 §2.4.7–2.4.8). Each message cites the section of the standard:
    • variable names (and FMI 3.0 aliases) are unique; FMI 3.0 value references are unique;
    • allowed combinations of causality and variability; only Real / Float32 / Float64 variables can be continuous;
    • allowed values of initial, and presence or absence of a start value;
    • derivative attributes and <ModelStructure> entries refer to existing variables;
    • <Outputs> / <Output> lists exactly the outputs; state derivatives have a derivative attribute.

With fmutool -check, any error logged by a checker makes the command exit with status 7.

docs.title: Running the Checker
docs.text:
CLIGUIPython API 
fmutool -input my_model.fmu -check

In fmutool-gui, click the Check FMU button after loading an FMU.

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import FMU
from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.checker import OperationGenericCheck

fmu = FMU("my_model.fmu")
check = OperationGenericCheck()
fmu.apply_operation(check)

if check.compliant_with_version:
    print(f"FMU is compliant with FMI {check.compliant_with_version}")
else:
    print("FMU is NOT compliant")

docs.title: Writing a Custom Checker
docs.text:
A checker is a class derived from OperationAbstract. Override the callback methods to inspect FMU attributes and ports:

import logging
from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.operations import OperationAbstract, ModelVariable

logger = logging.getLogger("fmu_manipulation_toolbox")


class CheckNamingConvention(OperationAbstract):
    """Check that all port names use snake_case."""

    def __repr__(self):
        return "Naming convention checker"

    def port_attrs(self, fmu_port: ModelVariable) -> int:
        name = fmu_port["name"]
        if name != name.lower():
            logger.warning(f"Port '{name}' is not snake_case")
        return 0

Save this file (e.g., my_checkers.py) anywhere on your system.

docs.title: From a Python file
docs.text:
Use add_from_file to load checkers at runtime before running fmutool:

from fmu_manipulation_toolbox.checker import add_from_file

add_from_file("path/to/my_checkers.py")

All classes that directly subclass OperationAbstract in the file will be automatically registered and executed during checks.

docs.title: Via entry points
docs.text:
You can also register checkers as Python package entry points using the fmu_manipulation_toolbox.checkers group in your setup.py or pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."fmu_manipulation_toolbox.checkers"]
my_checker = "my_package:get_checker_class"

A checker that cannot be imported, from a file or through an entry point, is reported as an error and skipped: the other checkers still run. This is the case of a checker written for version 1.x that still imports FMUPort, removed in 2.0: replace it by ModelVariable (see Writing Custom Operations).

docs.title: Command Line Interface (CLI) Usage Guide
docs.text: The command line offers complete and precise control over FMU Manipulation Toolbox, ideal for automation and batch processing.

docs.title: Available Commands
docs.text:
FMU Manipulation Toolbox provides four main commands:

Command Usage fmutool FMU analysis and manipulation fmucontainer FMU container creation fmusplit Extract FMUs from a container datalog2pcap Convert CAN datalog CSV to PCAP (experimental)

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text: fmutool -input <file.fmu> [options]

docs.title: Required Options
docs.text:
-input path/to/module.fmu

The FMU to analyze or modify.

docs.title: Save Options
docs.text:
-output path/to/module-modified.fmu

⚠️ Important: Without this option, no modifications are saved!

docs.title: Display FMU Summary
docs.text:
fmutool -input module.fmu -summary

Output: 

FMU Information:
  Name: module
  FMI Version: 2.0
  GUID: {abc-123-def}
  Number of variables: 42
  Number of parameters: 5
  Number of inputs: 10
  Number of outputs: 15

docs.title: Check FMI Compliance
docs.text:
fmutool -input module.fmu -check

Two built-in checkers are run, followed by the custom ones (see FMU Checker):

  • the XSD schema of the FMI version (every violation is reported, not only the first one);
  • the semantic rules that the schema cannot express: unique names and value references, allowed causality/variability/initial combinations, presence of start values, references between variables and in <ModelStructure>.

Each violation is logged as an error. If any checker logs an error, fmutool exits with status 7, after having performed the other requested actions (e.g. -output), so that -check can be used in CI.

docs.title: List All Ports in CSV
docs.text:
fmutool -input module.fmu -dump-csv ports_list.csv

Generated CSV content: 

name;newName;valueReference;causality;variability
Motor.Speed;Motor.Speed;0;input;continuous
Motor.Torque;Motor.Torque;1;output;continuous
Controller.Kp;Controller.Kp;2;parameter;fixed

docs.title: Remove Top-Level Hierarchy
docs.text:
Before: 

System.Motor.Speed
System.Controller.Gain

Command: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -remove-toplevel -output module-flat.fmu

After: 

Motor.Speed
Controller.Gain

docs.title: Merge First Level
docs.text:
Before: 

System.Motor.Speed
System.Controller.Gain

Command: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -merge-toplevel -output module-merged.fmu

After: 

System_Motor.Speed
System_Controller.Gain

docs.title: Remove Prefix
docs.text:
Before: 

_internal_Motor_Speed
_internal_Controller_Gain

Command: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -trim-until _ -output module-trimmed.fmu

After: 

internal_Motor_Speed
internal_Controller_Gain

docs.title: Rename from CSV File
docs.text:
Step 1: Create CSV 

fmutool -input module.fmu -dump-csv renaming.csv

Step 2: Edit CSV

Edit renaming.csv: 

name;newName;valueReference;causality;variability
Motor.Speed;Engine.Velocity;0;input;continuous
Motor.Torque;Engine.Force;1;output;continuous

Step 3: Apply modifications 

fmutool -input module.fmu -rename-from-csv renaming.csv -output module-renamed.fmu

Tip: Leaving newName empty removes the port!

docs.title: Filter by Regular Expression
docs.text:
Keep only matching ports: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -keep-only-regexp "^Motor\..*" -output module-motor.fmu

Remove matching ports: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -remove-regexp "^Internal\..*" -output module-clean.fmu

docs.title: Regular Expression Examples
docs.text:
# Keep everything starting with "Motor."
-keep-only-regexp "^Motor\..*"

# Remove everything containing "debug"
-remove-regexp ".*debug.*"

# Keep ports ending with "Temperature"
-keep-only-regexp ".*Temperature$"

# Remove ports starting with underscore
-remove-regexp "^_.*"

docs.title: Remove All Ports
docs.text:
fmutool -input module.fmu -remove-all -output module-empty.fmu

⚠️ Warning: This removes ALL ports! Use with filters.

docs.title: Operations on Parameters Only
docs.text:
List only parameters: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -only-parameters -dump-csv parameters.csv

Remove all parameters: 

fmutool -input module.fmu -only-parameters -remove-all -output module-no-params.fmu

docs.title: Operations on Inputs Only
docs.text:
# List inputs
fmutool -input module.fmu -only-inputs -dump-csv inputs.csv

# Rename inputs
fmutool -input module.fmu -only-inputs -rename-from-csv new_inputs.csv -output module.fmu

docs.title: Operations on Outputs Only
docs.text:
# List outputs
fmutool -input module.fmu -only-outputs -dump-csv outputs.csv

# Filter outputs
fmutool -input module.fmu -only-outputs -keep-only-regexp "^Result\." -output module.fmu

docs.title: Operations on Local Variables Only
docs.text:
# List local variables
fmutool -input module.fmu -only-locals -dump-csv locals.csv

# Remove all local variables
fmutool -input module.fmu -only-locals -remove-all -output module-no-locals.fmu

docs.title: Remove Sources
docs.text:
fmutool -input module.fmu -remove-sources -output module-no-src.fmu

Effect: The sources/ folder is removed from the FMU.

docs.title: Compile Sources
docs.text:
fmutool -input module.fmu -compile-sources -output module-compiled.fmu
